title: Green Customers, Faster Cycles? Product Innovation in Segmented Markets
affiliations: ESMT European School of Management and Technology and Nova School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Green Customers, Faster Cycles? Product Innovation in Segmented Markets
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Firms face growing pressure to invest in eco-innovation to reduce environmental impact. However, technological progress can also accelerate product introductions, shorten lifecycles, and intensify environmental concerns. We study how a monopolist determines the amount of investment in performance and environmental innovation and the timing of product launches, and how these choices jointly shape profitability and environmental outcomes across alternative market strategies. Methodology/results: We develop a unified infinite-horizon model in which a monopolist invests in per formance and environmental quality and periodically introduces durable products while forward-looking con sumers replace them under rational expectations. We characterize equilibria under three strategies: serving the entire market with performance-only products (mass market strategy), targeting eco-conscious consumers with products that embed environmental features (green market strategy), and offering a differentiated line tailored to both segments (differentiated market strategy). The equilibrium strategy depends critically on the size of the green customer segment and the relative efficiencies of performance and eco-innovation. Our analysis reveals that targeting green consumers can accelerate obsolescence and paradoxically increase en vironmental impact, whereas the mass market strategy may simultaneously yield the highest profit and the lowest environmental footprint. The differentiated market strategy, meanwhile, need not dominate in either dimension. Numerical experiments further illustrate how innovation elasticities, market composition, and production/disposal versus use-phase impacts influence both profitability and sustainability. Managerial implications: These findings inform managers on when and how to integrate eco-innovation into product portfolios and guide policymakers seeking to align environmental regulation with firm incentives. For managers, eco-variants are beneficial only when they appeal to a large customer base that highly values eco-features. For policymakers, incentive design must account for strategic replacement dynamics, which otherwise risk unintended environmental setbacks.

title: Monthly Recurring Donations Increase Charitable Giving

detail.title: Monthly Recurring Donations Increase Charitable Giving

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest with regard to this study
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a retrospective analysis of existing administrative data. No ethical/IRB review is required.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was financially supported by the AFP Foundation Levis Grant program.

detail.abstract: Using two large-scale data sets comprising hundreds of millions of charitable contribution transactions to tens of thousands of US charities, I quantify the relationship between monthly recurring charitable contributions and donor behavior. Compared to other donors, recurring donors are much more likely to give again in the future, much more likely to increase their giving, and are vastly more dependable for charitable fundraisers. These associations are not explained by the observable characteristics of recurring donors. All else equal, recurring monthly gifts are worth more than twice as much as non-recurring gifts to charities in terms of the present value of implied future giving.

title: Understanding Social Barriers to Renewable Electricity Adoption: Climate Change Skepticism and Resistance to Behavioural Change
affiliations: University of Murcia and Murcia University

detail.title: Understanding Social Barriers to Renewable Electricity Adoption: Climate Change Skepticism and Resistance to Behavioural Change

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the OPEN project, grant TED2021-131074B-I00 funded by MCIN/AEI/10.13039/501100011033

detail.abstract: The transition toward renewable energy is a cornerstone of European climate strategy under Directive (EU) 2023/2413. These requirements are directly reflected in national energy planning; for instance, Spain aims to achieve at least 81% renewable electricity generation by 2030. However, the success of these mandates depends on broad social acceptance and the mitigation of behavioural barriers, particularly Climate Change Skepticism. This study employs a contingent valuation approach to assess social demand among households in the Region of Murcia, Spain, where electricity is the dominant energy source. The results reveal a significant 44.59% protest response rate, reflecting substantial social resistance and a lack of social engagement. Among participating households, the mean willingness to pay (WTP) is €6.42 per month, representing an 8.36% increase over the average bill. By addressing population heterogeneity through Latent Class Cluster analysis, the study identifies four distinct segments based on socioeconomic characteristics and purchasing behaviour patterns. Variability in WTP is primarily driven by attitudes regarding anthropogenic responsibility and renewable energy efficacy. These findings suggest that generic awareness programs are insufficient; policy design must be tailored to specific social profiles, prioritizing communication on human impact and technical effectiveness to ensure a socially sustainable energy transition.

title: What is the value of attention? Supply and demand estimation of attention in a mobile app setting
affiliations: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: What is the value of attention? Supply and demand estimation of attention in a mobile app setting
detail.abstract: I study the digital market for attention in a freemium mobile game where users choose between paying with money or by watching 30-second video ads.Using unique event-level data, I estimate consumers’ supply elasticity of attention. In the aggregate, a one percent higher price increases the share of users watching videos as a payment by 2.2 percent. A substantial part is due to individual heterogeneity in tastes. When accounting for individual heterogeneity, the elasticity reduces to $0.5$. The individual elasticities vary throughout the day, peaking in the evening. Complementing the unique data on each play made by users, I use data on the revenue to the gaming company from showing ads. The data is on an individual and daily level, allowing me to match the individual supply elasticity with the revenue from showing ads to the same individual.I find advertisers pay more to show ads to individuals who are less likely to use ads as their payment method. The effect is stronger among Android users than iOS users.

title: Exporting, Wage Profiles, and Human Capital: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and Universidad Torcuato Di Tella

detail.title: Exporting, Wage Profiles, and Human Capital: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: Export activity shapes workers’ experience-wage profiles. Using employer-employee and customs data for Brazilian manufacturing, we document that workers’ experience-wage profiles are steeper at exporters than at non-exporters and, among exporters, steeper at exporters shipping to high-income destinations. We develop and quantify a model featuring worker-firm wage bargaining, export-market entry by multi-worker firms, and human capital accumulation by workers to interpret the data. Human capital growth can explain one-half of the differences in wage profiles between exporters and non-exporters. We show that increased human capital per worker can account for one-half of the overall gains in real income from trade openness.

detail.abstract: Family businesses (FBs) and co-branding represent two rich research domains that have witnessed substantial growth in both the volume and diversity of literature over the past decade. Despite this significant advancement, the absence of comprehensive reviews at the intersection of FBs and co-branding may lead to overlapping studies in the future, as each research domain tends to interpret results predominantly from its own unilateral perspective. Consequently, this study aims to provide a systematic review of the relationship between FBs and co-branding. Employing a combination of content analysis and bibliometric techniques, a total of 7,153 documents were extracted from databases including ScienceDirect, Emerald, Springer, and Wiley. After applying selection criteria, 6,157 documents were included in the analysis to ascertain publication rankings and identify key themes using VOSviewer software. Based on the findings, the authors address gaps in previous research and outline directions for future inquiry. In terms of theoretical contributions, this study pioneers applying qualitative (content analysis) and quantitative (bibliometric analysis) techniques to systematically review the interconnections between the literature on FBs and co-branding. From a practical perspective, FBs can leverage the co-branding process to enhance their effectiveness.

title: Talent Is Everywhere, Opportunity Is Not: Online Role Model Mentoring and Students’ Aspirations
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics, , University of Lausanne and

detail.title: Talent Is Everywhere, Opportunity Is Not: Online Role Model Mentoring and Students’ Aspirations
detail.abstract: Educational disparities often limit students' access to relatable role models, constraining their aspirations and educational outcomes. We design and implement the Online Role Model Mentoring Program (ORME), a scalable, low-cost intervention connecting middle school students with successful role models from similar backgrounds. Using a randomized controlled trial with over 450 students in Campania, Italy, we find that ORME improves students' beliefs about the returns to effort, increases alignment between aspirations and expectations, and boosts school effort. Treated students also become more academically ambitious: they are more likely to enroll in academically oriented tracks and perform better on standardized language tests. These findings show that brief online mentoring sessions can have a meaningful impact on students’ attitudes and choices at a critical stage of schooling, highlighting a promising tool to support students in low-opportunity contexts.

title: Tax Design, Pass-Through, and Incidence in Sports Betting
affiliations: and

detail.title: Tax Design, Pass-Through, and Incidence in Sports Betting
detail.abstract: In sports betting markets, the pass-through and incidence of taxation depends on the tax base. In Illinois, an excise tax on wagers passed through one-to-one to consumer prices, while taxes on gaming revenues do not pass through to prices. Instead, narrative evidence suggests that firms respond to revenue taxes by reducing marketing expenditures. We discuss the policy implications of these facts, which depend on whether there are distortions in sports betting consumption, and on the characteristics of bettors who respond to prices versus marketing.

title: The Future is Coming: Socioemotional Selectivity Theory and Temporal Agency

detail.title: The Future is Coming: Socioemotional Selectivity Theory and Temporal Agency
detail.abstract: When approaching the end of significant time intervals (e.g., one’s lifespan, career, college experience, etc.), people tend to forgo the desire to acquire knowledge and instead seek out experiences that are emotionally fulfilling. People often encode their experience of temporal passage in these intervals using metaphorical language that assigns agency to themselves or the event (e.g., we’re coming up on our vacation vs. our vacation is coming up). Embodiment theory suggests that our understanding of emotion and motion are intertwined, with positive feelings associated with approach and negative feelings associated with avoidance. This link can explain why agentic language is used within a temporal, and consequently, emotional, context. The reported study explores the relationship between imagined future life events and a communicator’s temporal agentic language use. Participants (N=327) were asked to imagine future life events (a relationship, a job, or a vacation) and describe their imagined experience at the beginning, middle, or end of the event (3 X 3 repeated measures factorial design). A reliable relationship between event component and agency assignment was observed. Specifically, communicators preferred to assign temporal agency to events when describing the end of an event than its beginning or middle, and preferred to assign temporal agency to themselves when describing the beginning of an event than it’s ending or middle. This finding suggests that participants, when faced with moments that are associated with mixed emotions (i.e., both positive and negative), prefer to convey the passage of time by assigning agency to the event itself.

title: Nominalization and Identity: Exploring the Impact of Linguistic Framing on Behavior and Self-Perception
affiliations: and

detail.title: Nominalization and Identity: Exploring the Impact of Linguistic Framing on Behavior and Self-Perception
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effects of linguistic framing, specifically the use of nouns versus verbs, on individuals' behavior and self-perception in activities related to reading and writing. Drawing upon the concept of noun essentialism, which suggests that nouns associated with an individual convey something intrinsic and enduring to their identity, this research explores the hypothesis that framing these activities with nouns (e.g., reader, writer) can increase effort for those who are primed with and accept these identity labels. Conversely, it also considers the possibility that such framing might reduce effort for those who are primed with and do not identify with the implied identity. The study presents two online experiments designed to test these hypotheses. Study 1 examines the impact of noun-based (e.g., Do you consider yourself a reader?) versus verb-based (e.g., Do you enjoy reading?) priming questions on participants' effort in a reading task, measured by their ability to answer comprehension questions and identify grammatical errors in a passage. Study 2 investigates the effect of similar noun-based (e.g., Do you consider yourself a writer?) and verb-based (e.g., Do you enjoy writing?) priming on the effort exerted in a writing task, measured through word count, writing completion time, and text readability (i.e., the grade level required to read a text). While prior research has indicated that noun framing can positively influence behaviors like voter turnout, the findings of the study reveal no significant differences in effort (as measured in Studies 1 and 2) between participants primed with noun-based versus verb-based questions. Additionally, Study 2 explored the potential influence of AI-generated responses on the writing task, noting a trend of higher AI use rate among participants who did not identify with the writer noun framing, although these differences were not statistically significant. Despite the lack of support for the initial hypotheses, the study contributes to the theoretical understanding of nominalization effects by suggesting that the persuasive advantage of nouns may be domain-specific and contingent on factors like identity salience and the competitive nature of the task.

title: Entrepreneurial Mindset on the Startup Survival Rates of Small Retail Businesses Inputs for Recommendations
affiliations: World Citi Colleges and World Citi Colleges

detail.title: Entrepreneurial Mindset on the Startup Survival Rates of Small Retail Businesses Inputs for Recommendations
detail.abstract: This study examined the influence of the entrepreneurial mindset on the survival rates of small retail startups in Mandaluyong City, Philippines, focusing on the traits of opportunity recognition, innovation, and risk-taking. Using a descriptive-correlational design, data were collected from 100 proprietors of convenience stores, boutiques, and specialty shops in Barangay Barangka through a structured questionnaire based on the Ghent Entrepreneurial Mindset Scale (GEMS). Descriptive statistics revealed a moderate entrepreneurial mindset (grand mean = 3.02), with innovation (M = 3.15) and opportunity recognition (M = 3.14) rated highest, while financial management (M = 2.81) and risk-taking (M = 2.92) emerged as weaker areas. Respondents reported significant challenges, particularly lack of mentorship (M = 2.76) and difficulty adapting to consumer preferences (M = 2.72). Pearson correlation and ANOVA analyses showed no significant relationships or differences in mindset assessments across demographic profiles (age, gender, education, years in business, business type), accepting both null hypotheses (HO1: p > 0.05; HO2: p > 0.05). Linear regression confirmed that mindset does not significantly predict years in operation (β = -0.282, p = 0.855). Anchored on Entrepreneurial Mindset Theory and the Resource-Based View, the findings suggest that while a moderate entrepreneurial mindset supports adaptability and resilience, systemic barriers limit its full impact on survival. Recommendations include targeted financial literacy training, mentorship programs, and policy support through DTI aligned initiatives to enhance startup sustainability in urban retail contexts.

detail.title: Firms and the Gender Wage Gap: A Comparison of Eleven Countries

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-24
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We quantify the role of gender-specific firm wage premiums in explaining the private-sector gender gap in hourly wages using a harmonized research design across 11 matched employer-employee datasets — ten European countries and Washington State, USA. These premiums contribute to the gender wage gap through two channels: women’s concentration in lower-paying firms (sorting) and women receiving lower premiums than men within the same firm (pay-setting).We find that firm wage premiums account for 10 to 30 percent of the gender wage gap. While both mechanisms matter, sorting is the predominant driver of the firm contribution to the gender wage gap in most countries. We document three patterns that are broadly consistent across countries: (1) women’s sorting into lower-paying firms increases with age; (2) women are more concentrated in low-paying firms with a high share of part-time workers; and (3) women receive about 90 percent of the rents that men receive from firm surplus gains.

title: Algorithmic Advancements and Workforce Dynamics in the Gig Economy: Evidence from the On-Demand Delivery Market
affiliations: , University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business, Fudan University - School of Management and Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems

detail.title: Algorithmic Advancements and Workforce Dynamics in the Gig Economy: Evidence from the On-Demand Delivery Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines how algorithmic advancements shape worker productivity and labor market dynamics in the gig economy. While prior research has emphasized technology's effects in traditional labor markets, the implications of continuous algorithmic advancement in the gig economy remain insufficiently understood. Using four years of comprehensive rider-level data from a major on-demand food delivery platform, we develop and estimate a structural model that links heterogeneous productivity responses, dynamic participation choices, and market-level demand-supply conditions. We find that improvements in dispatch and routing algorithms compress skill gaps by disproportionately raising the productivity of low-skilled riders, thereby reducing the marginal value of specialized domain skills. This skill-equalizing effect triggers asymmetric participation responses in a flexible labor environment: low-skilled riders increase engagement, whereas high-skilled riders reduce participation and are more likely to exit over time. Despite the resulting compositional decline in traditional skills, overall delivery performance improves and outcome dispersion widens, driven by emerging heterogeneity in workers' ability to leverage algorithmic support. These findings reveal a new mechanism through which iterative algorithmic systems reshape labor markets: they equalize traditional skill premiums while generating new productivity stratification plausibly rooted in algorithm literacy. We discuss implications for platform design and labor governance in technology-mediated work.

title: Not All Good Deeds Look Alike: Configuring CSR and Firm Country of Origin Signals for Recruitment Success in Emerging Markets
affiliations: , University of Fribourg,  and

detail.title: Not All Good Deeds Look Alike: Configuring CSR and Firm Country of Origin Signals for Recruitment Success in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: This study explores how foreign firms can optimize their CSR strategies to attract talent in emerging markets, offering a more nuanced understanding of CSR's role in international recruitment beyond conventional "net effect" explanations. While causal complexity is considered a ubiquitous feature underlying international business, much of the existing research neglects a multi-level perspective and either isolates specific CSR dimensions or treats it as a uniform construct. Such approaches neglect both CSR’s multifaceted nature and the practical reality that firms, operating with limited resources, must determine which CSR dimensions to prioritize in different contexts. Applicants, in turn, evaluate a bundle of signals, drawing from various CSR dimensions and other meso- and macro-level factors. To address these gaps, this study employs an experimental design and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine the interplay between firm-level CSR and country-level factors—particularly the firm’s country of origin—in a configurational approach. The results demonstrate how firm-level and country-level factors combine to shape applicants’ outcomes that cannot be adequately explained by factors at any single level of analysis in isolation. These insights offer compelling theoretical and managerial implications, underscoring the strategic importance of aligning and configuring CSR activities to the firm’s country of origin, thereby enabling more effective resource allocation and enhanced recruitment outcomes in international markets.

title: H-1B Visa Program, Visa Cap and Foreign Worker Earnings
affiliations: Department of Economics, Rutgers University, Newark and Kent State University

detail.title: H-1B Visa Program, Visa Cap and Foreign Worker Earnings

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using various years of data from the National Survey of College Survey we examine the earnings of work visa immigrants who entered the U.S. during the various H-1B cap periods and whether the cap was binding or not at the time of their entry. For work visa entrants in the non-academic sector as well as from cap bound countries, we find that earning premium relative to college graduate natives ranges between 17%-25% if the immigrants entered the U.S. during the initial period of H-1B and during the later binding cap periods. This premium is lost if immigrants first entered on H-1B during the non-binding period. Compared to pre 1990 work immigrants we find there is a drop in earnings for immigrants who entered on H-1B during the non binding period. This is not seen in the academic sector and for five cap exempt countries, where cap is not relevant. Our findings are driven by the H-1B program involving staffing agencies hiring of low ability workers and workers facing wage suppression with limited job mobility. Work visa entrants may also face scarring in the labor market because of lack of U.S. education experience. We do not find this drop in earning for student visa entrants who are admitted by the university selection process.

title: Rethinking stocking density: Biological and operational tradeoffs of splitting oysters (Crassostrea virginica) at different trigger densities in off-bottom oyster aquaculture
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Rethinking stocking density: Biological and operational tradeoffs of splitting oysters (Crassostrea virginica) at different trigger densities in off-bottom oyster aquaculture
detail.abstract: Successful management in off-bottom oyster farming relies on controlling crowding as oysters grow. Though frequently studied in terms of initial stocking density, oyster densities must later be reduced by “splitting” into additional containers. The density at which these splits occur—here termed trigger density—has not been quantitatively evaluated. In this study, we tested how three trigger densities (25%, 50%, and 75% of container volumetric capacity) affected biological performance and operational demands across a 14-month oyster grow-out cycle in the York River (Virginia, USA). When oyster densities reached treatment-specific thresholds, they were size-graded, split, and reset to a standardized initial stocking density (10% volumetric capacity) across additional containers. Despite a disease-related mortality event that reduced survival across all treatments, trigger density significantly affected the quantity and qualities of oysters produced. Market yield declined with increasing trigger density, with the lowest trigger density producing approximately 6% more market-sized oysters than the highest. Survival also tended to be higher when splitting at lower trigger densities. Market-sized oysters from the lowest trigger density developed deeper cups, a tendency toward wider fans, and reduced shell height relative to those from the highest trigger density, likely reflecting effects from increased handling. Operationally, the lowest trigger density required three splits and approximately 2.3-fold more labor and 3.5-fold more grow-out containers than the highest trigger density which was split once. These results demonstrate that trigger density is a distinct, consequential component of density management and therefore carries implications for optimizing production in commercial off-bottom farming systems.

title: "An Analysis Study on the Implementation of the Teacher's Code of Ethics"

detail.title: "An Analysis Study on the Implementation of the Teacher's Code of Ethics"
detail.abstract: The writer expresses profound gratitude to God Almighty for His blessings and grace, which have made it possible to complete this paper titled “Analysis of the Implementation of the Teacher’s Code of Ethics” on time. This paper was prepared as part of the course Ethics of the Teaching Profession, with the intention of enhancing understanding of the importance of ethical principles in education, especially within the teaching profession. The purpose of writing this paper is to provide a clearer and more in-depth explanation of how teachers are expected to perform their duties based on moral and ethical values. Furthermore, this paper also aims to explore the various factors that influence the application of the code of ethics and to highlight several cases of ethical violations that have occurred in the field, serving as valuable reflection material for educators and future teachers.

title: Temperature Shocks and Climate Change: A Conceptual Analysis

detail.title: Temperature Shocks and Climate Change: A Conceptual Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately modeling and estimating climate change damages. Time series approaches rely on weather shocks, while cross-sectional analyses capture climatic differences but suffer from omitted variable bias. Climate is defined as the statistical pattern of weather that persists over time and allows for adaptation, unlike unpredictable weather realizations. To assess econometric approaches, I (i) integrate forward-looking adaptation into a full-fledged integrated assessment model of climate change permitting an analytic solution and (ii) generalize the insights based on a dynamic stochastic envelope argument. I show how a carefully designed time series (or panel) estimation strategy can comprehensively identify the costs of climate change, including the indirect identification of unobserved adaptation costs. The paper also presents the first explicit formula for This result is not only insightful in its own right but also valuable for clarifying and refining prevailing envelope-theorem arguments in the literature and for emphasizing that adaptation costs are part of the social cost of carbon.

title: Demand for Health Insurance: Financial and Informational Role of Informal Networks
affiliations: University of Warwick, IIM Calcutta and University of Calcutta

detail.title: Demand for Health Insurance: Financial and Informational Role of Informal Networks
detail.abstract: We study why free public health insurance in India exhibits persistently low utilisation despite high out of pocket health expenses. In the context of the Arogyasri program in Andhra Pradesh, we distinguish the roles of informal financial and information networks in shaping adoption. Empirically, households embedded in financial networks show higher take-up and utilisation, while information networks have no effect. To explain this pattern, we develop a simple theoretical framework in which informal financial networks act as mutual insurance: because members bear each other’s uninsured losses, the network has an incentive to push all members to enrol when the expected cost of shocks exceeds enrolment transaction costs. This generates corner solutions for network members and interior solutions for non-members, consistent with observed bimodal take-up patterns. The model clarifies why financial—but not informational—ties complement public insurance and highlights community-based mechanisms for increasing adoption.

title: High-Risk Drivers and Road-Safety Governance in Italy: A Behavioural and Policy Perspective
affiliations: University of Florence,  and University of Florence

detail.title: High-Risk Drivers and Road-Safety Governance in Italy: A Behavioural and Policy Perspective
detail.abstract: This study uses an integrated analysis of survey data from 1,060 participants to examine driver attitudes and behaviours regarding road safety in Italy. Cluster analysis identified distinct driver profiles and significant geographical disparities. A high-risk subgroup (25% of respondents) was found, characterized by high self-confidence and low responsibility; younger age emerged as a key correlate. The misalignment between perceived and actual safety highlights the need for evidence-based policies. The study advocates an integrated approach combining targeted education, data-driven enforcement, and strategic infrastructure investment to advance Vision Zero goals.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the potential of birth control policies to address socioeconomic challenges in Africa, such as entrenched poverty and slow economic growth. Many African countries face obstacles in fully implementing socioeconomic rights, leaving populations particularly children vulnerable to deprivation, limited educational opportunities, inadequate healthcare, and violations of their rights to protection and dignity. The study examines these issues within international and regional human rights frameworks, including the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, and the Maputo Protocol, evaluating both the extent of protections and state enforcement practices. The paper considers whether population management strategies, including birth limitation measures, could support existing development efforts by alleviating pressures on public services, improving health and education outcomes, and promoting fairer access to resources. Comparative examples illustrate potential benefits while highlighting the importance of safeguarding fundamental human rights. Concluding with actionable recommendations, the study advocates for integrating population management policies into broader socioeconomic development initiatives, consistent with Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals. When implemented alongside comprehensive socioeconomic reforms, such measures can enhance children's welfare, protect rights, and contribute to sustainable growth across African states.

detail.title: Determining Factors of Successful Commercial Banks in Implementing Sustainable Finance Policy in Indonesia

publicationDetails.detailsText: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development, 18 (12), 1369-1388, 2025.
publicationDetails.journalName: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development

detail.abstract: This study aims to determine the effectiveness of the implementation of a long-term policy, namely the Sustainable Finance (SF) policy made by the OJK (the Indonesia Financial Services Authority), especially in the initial phase of implementation. This study tries to answer whether an increase in a bank's perception of SF policy will be followed by a positive attitude towards the policy. Furthermore, this positive attitude will also be followed by proper actions to implement policy. This study also looks at whether the consideration of the size of the bank's business moderates the bank's perception of the bank's attitude and the bank's attitude towards the bank's actions to implement sustainable financial policy. This research also explores the bank's perception of the determinants of bank success in implementing SF policy. The combination method was used in this study. The quantitative method approach with one sample test and Structural Equation Model-Partial Least Square (SEM-PLS) and the qualitative method approach with Focus Group Discussion (FGD) were analyzed using NVivo. The results of statistical tests show that the level of bank perception of OJK's sustainable financial policy positively influences bank attitudes. Likewise, the bank's positive attitude towards SF policy positively affects the bank's actions. Bank size is not proven to moderate the positive influence of perception on attitudes and attitudes toward bank actions in implementing SF policy. A descriptive analysis of the bank's sustainability report shows that both large-and small-scale banks have a balanced response quality. The survey and FGD results show the bank's top management support, strengthening bank human resources, and appropriate incentives from the OJK and the government are very important to ensure the successful implementation of SF policy.

title: A Policy Reversal as Structural Break: A Lesson from China’s Land Lease Financing for Infrastructure
affiliations: Syracuse University,  and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE)

detail.title: A Policy Reversal as Structural Break: A Lesson from China’s Land Lease Financing for Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Land-based revenues as a fiscal instrument to finance infrastructure tie public investment to real estate markets, where demand fluctuations cause fiscal consequences. This paper takes policy reversals as structural breaks and examines their impacts on infrastructure investment. We dissect China’s 2016 policy reversal that disallowed developers to finance land purchase with debt, causing sharp declines in local government land revenues, slashing their fiscal base for infrastructure investment. Using prefecture-level panel data and continuous difference-in-differences identification, we estimate the reversal reduced land-lease revenues by 55%. Two-stage least squares estimates suggest a 10% land-revenue decline translates into 6.6% investment reduction. Decomposing the funding sources show that 70% of the decline stems from contractions in local self-financing and borrowings by local financing vehicles, and resource reallocations within these financing vehicles amplify the impacts of the structural break. The lesson is: policy regime stability is vital to fiscal systems that rely on land-based revenues.

detail.abstract: The urgency of transitioning to renewable energy (RE) is intensifying in response to escalating climate change risks, energy security challenges, and volatile global economic conditions. As one of the largest energy consumers in Southeast Asia, Indonesia stands at a pivotal juncture in its efforts to reduce dependence on fossil fuels while meeting growing domestic energy demands. Despite its abundant renewable energy potential, investment and infrastructure development remain significantly below expectations, hindering progress toward national energy objectives. To address these challenges, this study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of peer-reviewed publications from Scopus-indexed journals published between 2019 and 2024 to examine the impact of renewable energy investment on three critical dimensions: economic growth, environmental sustainability, and energy resilience. Guided by the PRISMA framework and applying structured inclusion and exclusion criteria, 56 high-quality articles were selected for in-depth analysis. The literature is categorized into three thematic areas: (i) Renewable Energy Investment (REI) and Economic Growth, (ii) REI and Environmental Sustainability, and (iii) Energy Resilience and Investment.

detail.abstract:
Healthcare organizations face escalating workplace violence, contested clinical encounters, and documentation disputes while operating under stringent privacy and regulatory obligations. Traditional incident reporting systems and fixed surveillance technologies are often retrospective, incomplete, or insufficiently contextual to support prevention, training, and quality improvement. In response, some health systems have explored body-worn cameras (BWCs) as a supplemental safety and accountability tool, particularly in high-risk clinical settings. However, the use of BWCs in healthcare presents substantial legal, ethical, and operational challenges related to patient privacy, consent, labor surveillance, equity, and data security. 

This paper proposes a compliance-forward governance framework for the ethical implementation of body-worn cameras in healthcare. Grounded in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), applicable state consent laws, workplace violence prevention guidance, and accreditation standards, the framework emphasizes narrowly defined use cases, event-based activation, restricted recording zones, consent workflows, retention limits, and auditable oversight. The paper further introduces a novel administrative role, the Clinical Recording Compliance Auditor (CRCA), to institutionalize governance, monitoring, and accountability. By centering regulatory compliance and ethical restraint, this framework seeks to mitigate foreseeable risks while supporting patient and staff safety.

title: A Complex-Plane Representation of Financial Cycles: Spiral Dynamics, Phase Misalignment, and Early-Warning Indicators
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: A Complex-Plane Representation of Financial Cycles: Spiral Dynamics, Phase Misalignment, and Early-Warning Indicators
detail.abstract:
We propose a parsimonious geometric framework for analyzing the joint dynamics of real economic activity and private-sector credit by representing the macroeconomy as a complex-valued variable Z(t) = R(t) + i C(t), where R(t) is real GDP and C(t) is the credit-to-GDP ratio (or total private credit). Using Euler's formula, the natural evolution of the system traces logarithmic spirals in the complex plane. The spiral expansion rate b = (γζ)/ω and the imbalance angle θ(t) = arctan(C(t)/R(t)) emerge as intuitive, interpretable indicators of financial fragility.
On quarterly data from 18 advanced and emerging economies (1990–2024), periods of
significantly positive b and rising θ systematically precede systemic banking and sovereign
debt crises by 4–10 quarters. A simple panel logit using only θ, dθ/dt, and b achieves an
AUC of 0.81 out-of-sample, comparable to benchmark machine-learning models (LSTM,
XGBoost) and superior to the Basel III credit-to-GDP gap in lead time and interpretability.
The framework offers a visually compelling synthesis of Minsky’s financial instability
hypothesis with complex systems theory while remaining fully transparent and replicable.

title: The Legal Prohibition of Hoarding Money in Islamic Jurisprudence and Its Implications for Monetary Policies

detail.title: The Legal Prohibition of Hoarding Money in Islamic Jurisprudence and Its Implications for Monetary Policies
detail.abstract:
Introduction and Objectives: The development of effective monetary policies within an Islamic economic framework necessitates grounding policy design in the core principles of Shari’ah. One such principle, introduced and examined in this research, is the “Principle of Connectivity and Fluidity of Money.” This principle asserts that money should continuously facilitate real economic activity and must be safeguarded from two forms of deviation: hoarding (Kanz) and entrapment in speculative financial cycles. Consequently, for monetary instruments to be compatible with Islamic jurisprudence, they must inherently possess both potential and actual liquidity.

The jurisprudential basis for this principle is derived from several interrelated concepts: the Theory of Vicegerency (Istikhlāf), which frames human stewardship over wealth; the notion of barakah or blessing in productive assets (nama’); and the Shari’ah objective of promoting wealth circulation, facilitating trade, and supporting production. The principle of monetary fluidity is operationalized via two pillars: (1) the prohibition against removing money from the productive economic cycle, clarified through the detailed jurisprudential analysis of Kanz (hoarding), and (2) the obligation of Zakāt (alms) as a mechanism to enforce circulation.

The main aim of this research is to provide a comprehensive examination of Kanz from both jurisprudential and exegetical perspectives, to analyze Qur’anic verse 9:34, and to identify contemporary manifestations of hoarding in modern economies. Additionally, the study explores the implications of these findings for the formulation of monetary policy within an Islamic system. The primary question addressed is whether the prohibition of Kanz is absolute or conditional upon the payment of Zakāt.

title: Industrial Intelligence Promotes Supply Chain Collaboration: Mechanism and Micro-Evidence
affiliations: Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS)

detail.title: Industrial Intelligence Promotes Supply Chain Collaboration: Mechanism and Micro-Evidence
detail.abstract:
Intelligent manufacturing is reshaping the landscape of traditional industrial chains; however, no research has yet systematically examined whether industrial intelligence affects the linkage structure of industrial chains. This paper utilizes annual report data of Chinese listed manufacturing firms and constructs a measurement index for the intelligence level of manufacturing enterprises through text analysis methods. On this basis, it empirically tests the impact of industrial intelligence on industrial chain collaboration.

The results indicate that industrial intelligence significantly promotes industrial chain collaboration, and this conclusion remains valid after a series of robustness tests. Mechanism tests reveal that reducing transaction costs and improving operational efficiency are important mechanisms by which industrial intelligence fosters supply chain collaboration. Heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that the promotional effect of industrial intelligence on supply chain collaboration is more pronounced in industries with stronger bargaining power and longer production chains, as well as in regions with superior digital infrastructure and higher degrees of industrial agglomeration. Extended research finds that the promotional effect of industrial intelligence on supply chain collaboration is endogenously driven by market competition pressure.

This paper comprehensively elucidates the intrinsic logic between industrial intelligence and industrial chain collaboration, enriches and deepens the research on factors influencing industrial chain collaboration with the theme of technological progress, and provides important references for accelerating the promotion of new industrialization, building a modern industrial system, and constructing a manufacturing powerhouse.

detail.abstract: Saving for the third age is extremely important in the conditions of an uncertainty in the global economy, unfavorable demographic trends and the related problem of fiscal imbalances. In order to improve the sustainability of the Croatian three-pillar pension system, there have been recent attempts to significantly increase the role of voluntary pension insurance and other forms of saving for the third age. The aim of such measures is to reduce the increasing dependence of pension beneficiaries on payments from the state budget and to achieve a more sustainable pension system. Measures to encourage voluntary saving in Croatia are the state incentives for the insured and the tax benefits for employers. Despite the numerous investment advantages and government incentives for this form of saving, voluntary pension funds in Croatia are still among the least developed institutional investors, considering the amount of assets and the number of members. The question arises as to the reasons for the relative disregard of these financial institutions and the low interest of the working population in Croatia. The aim of this paper is to analyze the performance of voluntary pension funds and identify the reasons for the insufficient capitalised savings in the third pension pillar in Croatia.

detail.title: Strategic Adaptation of Cashless Banking Sector in Region V: Basis for Enhancement Plan
detail.abstract: The rapid rise of financial technology (fintech) has reshaped the global banking sector, accelerating the transition toward a cashless economy through innovations such as mobile banking, e-wallets, and online payment platforms. In the Philippines, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has taken an active role in promoting digital transformation through initiatives such as the Digital Payments Transformation Roadmap 2020–2023. These efforts significantly increased the adoption of digital payments nationwide, contributing to the broader goal of financial inclusion. In Region V, banks and their clients are gradually shifting toward digital transactions. This transition presents both opportunities and challenges. While cashless systems offer convenience, efficiency, and reduced operational costs, they also expose clients to measurable concerns such as cybersecurity risks, varying system usability, digital literacy gaps, and trust issues. Since adoption depends on these quantifiable factors, assessing them provides a way to evaluate how well banks are adapting to the demands of a cashless economy. The present study adopts a quantitative approach to measure adoption rate, usage frequency, and satisfaction level among banking clients. By focusing on these indicators, the study aims to generate evidence-based insights that will guide banks in enhancing their digital strategies and align with the BSP’s vision of a financially inclusive and digitally empowered Philippines.

title: Structural Change and Spatial Concentration of High-income Earners: Evidence from French Regions since 1960

detail.title: Structural Change and Spatial Concentration of High-income Earners: Evidence from French Regions since 1960
detail.abstract: This article shows that the spatial dispersion of high-income earners across French regions follows an inverted U-shape between 1960 and 2019. Dispersion declined from the early 1960s to around 2000, driven by strong regional convergence in employment structures: the fastest deindustrialization occurred in manufacturing-intensive regions, while laggard regions expanded both manufacturing and services. Since the early 2000s, dispersion has risen again as convergence in services stopped and high-skilled services increasingly clustered in large urban areas. High earners were initially over-represented in major cities and the industrial Northeast; today in major cities and Swiss-border regions.

title: Medical Errors: Impact of Apology and Admission on the Resolution and Compensation of Claims

detail.title: Medical Errors: Impact of Apology and Admission on the Resolution and Compensation of Claims
detail.abstract: Studies investigating the impact of apologies and admission of responsibility for medical errors have been primarily observational, making it hard to attach a causal effect to the admission of responsibility and apologies. Second, most research on the settlement of medical malpractice cases were conducted in the US, with its particular litigation laws and culture. In this multi-jurisdictional study, we investigate the impact of apology and admission of responsibility on preferred resolution and compensation of claims. Employing a vignette design, we examine, among a sample of 327 respondents from 10 different countries, whether admission and apology by the doctor impact respondents' preference for resolution through a civil court case, mediation or a disciplinary board, as well as preferred damages for pain and suffering. Admission and apology by the physician in the vignette did not impact respondents' preference for settlement through a civil court case or mediation, nor did it affect the amount respondents found suitable compensation for pains and damages. We perceived the absence of an apology as particularly aggravating. Thematic analysis of open answers reveals that the impact of admission and apology differs for the three resolution modes and is often contextual and conditional. Future (vignette) studies should investigate whether different cases of medical errors yield similar results and whether more knowledgeable or experienced respondents (such as lawyers) would have other preferences and arguments.

title: Testing Structural Invariance Across AI Reasoning Systems

detail.title: Testing Structural Invariance Across AI Reasoning Systems
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a structural invariant governing reasoning collapse in humans also governs collapse dynamics in artificial reasoning systems. Large language models were subjected to a bistable invariant architecture defined by mathematically specified thresholds in evaluative load, independence drift, and structured entropy. Across multiple architectures, systems displayed the same stable, ambiguity, and collapse regimes predicted by the invariant. These findings provide initial evidence for crosssubstrate structural invariance.

title: A Dynamical Systems Architecture for Reasoning Stability and Abrupt Mode Switching in AI and Human Cognition

detail.title: A Dynamical Systems Architecture for Reasoning Stability and Abrupt Mode Switching in AI and Human Cognition
detail.abstract: This working paper introduces a unified dynamical-systems architecture that explains abrupt transitions in reasoning stability, including evaluative collapse, delayed recovery, and reorganizing trajectories observed in both artificial and human cognition. The model formalizes how evaluative load, independence-state drift, and structured entropy interact through a mathematical invariant whose switching thresholds generate discrete changes in reasoning mode. By specifying an invariant, drift measure, and hysteresis thresholds, the framework distinguishes stable reasoning, ambiguity drift, and collapse basins, and it provides a way to forecast transitions before they occur. A worked numerical example illustrates how small changes in the system's parameters can trigger regime shifts, and how recovery follows a different threshold than collapse. The architecture is directly implementable in artificial reasoning systems and offers a structural template for empirical work on human cognition and organizational decision processes under pressure. It is intended as a platform for testing stability control in AI inference, for modeling evaluative narrowing and recovery in human reasoning, and for analyzing collapse and reorganization dynamics in institutional settings.

title: How to Use the Sharpe Ratio (Seminar Slides)
affiliations: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Cornell University - Operations Research & Industrial Engineering

detail.title: How to Use the Sharpe Ratio (Seminar Slides)
detail.abstract:
•One of the most widely accepted measures of investment efficiency is the Sharpe ratio, which expresses excess return relative to volatility
•While the Sharpe ratio is reported ubiquitously in academic and practitioner publications, the inference done on it is often wrong
•Common mistakes include:
–Comparing annualized Sharpe ratios, without taking into account its sampling variance
–Using generic statistical tests that make unrealistic assumptions, such as i.i.d. Normal returns
–Neglect minimum sample lengths and the power of the test
–Interpreting the rejection of the null hypothesis as evidence that the null hypothesis is likely false
–Ignoring multiple testing corrections
•In this seminar, we review how to use the Sharpe ratio for making investment decisions within a sound statistical framework

title: Measuring Global Supply Chain Disruptions: A Systematic Review of Existing Indexes and Indicators
affiliations: Global Supply Chain and Independent author

detail.title: Measuring Global Supply Chain Disruptions: A Systematic Review of Existing Indexes and Indicators
detail.abstract: Global supply chains have experienced repeated disruptions driven by geopolitical tensions, pandemics, natural disasters, transportation bottlenecks, and labor shortages. Numerous indicators and indexes attempt to measure these disruptions, including freight rates, delivery-time metrics, trade-flow indicators, commodity market signals, and event-driven risk measures. However, these tools were developed independently, rely on heterogeneous data sources, and capture only partial aspects of disruption, resulting in a fragmented measurement landscape. This paper presents a systematic review of major indicators and indexes used to quantify global supply chain disruptions. Using a structured multi-phase search strategy, it analyzes peer-reviewed studies, institutional reports, and industry metrics across six domains: transportation and logistics, production and suppliers, trade flows, labor markets, commodity and energy markets, and geopolitical or policy shocks. For each measure, the review summarizes its purpose, data foundation, methodology, strengths, and limitations. The findings show that existing indicators provide useful but siloed insights and do not capture disruptions across all domains in an integrated way. Addressing this gap is essential for improving forecasting, risk management, and resilience planning. The review synthesizes fragmented measurement approaches and proposes the Global Supply Chain Disruption Index (GSCDI) framework as a unified conceptual foundation for future empirical development.

title: Reassessing Accounting Anomalies in an Investable U.S. Equity Universe
affiliations: , University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne), University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne) and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Reassessing Accounting Anomalies in an Investable U.S. Equity Universe
detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the profitability of 25 accounting-based signals in the U.S. equity market over the period 1963-2024. Using CRSP returns, Compustat annual fundamentals, and the CRSP-Compustat Merged database, we construct a point-in-time panel of U.S. common stocks and implement conservative filters (NYSE P20 size breakpoint, minimum price of $5, and historical return requirements) to approximate a liquid, investable universe. We form value-weighted and equal-weighted long-short decile portfolios, correct for delisting bias, and evaluate performance using Fama-French six-factor regressions with Newey-West standard errors and an explicit |t| > 3 benchmark to account for multiple testing. Our results show that, once we focus on value-weighted portfolios in this liquid universe, most fundamental signals fail to deliver statistically significant alphas and appear largely absorbed by modern risk factors. A small subset of strategies remains economically meaningful. A "Cash Cushion" measure of financial flexibility yields an annualised six-factor alpha of roughly 5%, gross of transaction costs, with t ≈ 2.1 in the full sample, and somewhat larger point estimates in the post-1980 and post-2000 subperiods; we interpret this as a promising, but not definitive, candidate for a defensive premium. By contrast, several growth and quality-related signals-most notably ROIC Momentum and Intangible Power-earn large and robustly negative alphas with |t| > 3, suggesting that the market tends to overpay for certain improvement and intangible-capital stories. We highlight that our deeper analysis of Cash Cushion and ROIC Momentum is conducted ex post, based on their full-sample performance. Overall, the evidence points to limited scope for robust, value-weighted alpha from standard accounting signals in U.S. equities, with the most compelling opportunities arising on the short side rather than from long-only fundamental tilts.

title: Asset Allocation with a Carbon Objective
affiliations: , University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne), University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne), University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne) and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Asset Allocation with a Carbon Objective
detail.abstract: Can deep portfolio decarbonisation be achieved without eroding financial performance? Using monthly returns and annual CO 2 data for more than 600 North-American equities (2014-2024), we extend mean-variance optimisation into a three-dimensional (u, o, carbon) space and evaluate five allocations: (i) an unconstrained minimum-variance portfolio; (ii) a value-weighted benchmark; (iii) a minimum-variance design capped at 50 % of its own footprint; (iv) a benchmark-neutral strategy that halves the benchmark footprint subject to a tracking-error budget; and (v) a dynamic Net-Zero portfolio imposing a 10 % yearly emissions decline. Across the sample, carbon-constrained strategies cut financed emissions by 20-50 % while delivering Sharpe ratios statistically indistinguishable from-sometimes superior to-the unconstrained benchmark. Their annualised tracking errors cluster around 4.9 %, well above the 0.30-0.50 % floor to prevent index replication. Only the Net-Zero design at the shortest look-back window (48 months) briefly peaks at 7.4 % before reverting below 5 % as the estimation horizon lengthens. Early cuts of up to roughly 50 % in carbon footprint appear to entail little to no performance penalty, whereas deeper reductions trade off transparently against the tracking-error "budget". The Net-Zero trajectory remains consistent with a 1.5 • C carbon budget while preserving almost the entire equity risk premium, offering counter-evidence to the notion of an inevitable sustainability tax. Overall, the evidence shows that ambitious, Paris-aligned decarbonisation can be embedded in mainstream portfolios through explicit tracking-error limits, offering investors a coherent and auditable framework for aligning assets with the Paris Agreement while maintaining competitive performance.

title: The Epistemic Sabotage; Misinformation and the Erosion of Democratic Power

detail.title: The Epistemic Sabotage; Misinformation and the Erosion of Democratic Power
detail.abstract: This paper explores how misinformation acts as a structural force undermining the epistemic conditions necessary for democratic legitimacy. Drawing on Robert Dahl's criteria of effective participation and enlightened understanding, along with classical liberal conceptions of consent, the paper argues that democracy cannot meaningfully function when citizens form political preferences under distorted or asymmetrically curated information conditions. Using the United States as the central case, the paper examines how state narratives, media ecosystems, and algorithmic infrastructures converge to shape public perception on issues ranging from foreign policy to national security, to racialised conflict. Instead of treating misinformation as an incidental by-product of digital media, the analysis here frames it as a systemic feature of contemporary governance-that is, one wherein existing power hierarchies are iteratively secured amidst an outward appearance of pluralism and free choice. The paper concludes that misinformation engenders a self-reinforcing feedback loop wherein the misinformed citizenry unwittingly stabilises the very institutions limiting their autonomy, leaving the democratic order procedurally intact but substantively weakened.

detail.abstract: Fiscal policy is usually announced before it is implemented, and such announcements can affect macroeconomic conditions regardless of whether the announced measures are actually implemented. In this paper, I construct two new quarterly fiscal announcement indices-one specific to public spending and the other to taxation-based on press reports from four major euro area economies: Spain, France, Italy, and Germany (1999-2025). Using large language models, whose classifications I validate manually, I systematically code each news item according to the fiscal stance it conveys, the responsible institutional level and the type of communication. I then incorporate these specific government expenditure and taxation indices into a battery of bayesian vector autoregressive models, estimated both by country and in a grouped panel framework, with recursive identification. I demonstrate that, consistently across the four countries-although the responses for Germany are somewhat less stable-signals of increased public spending anticipate actual increases in government expenditure and generate clear and persistent expansions in GDP and consumption, while announcements of tax increases boost tax revenues but produce more moderate and shorter-lived contractions. Overall, the results confirm that press reports contain useful information for identifying the shocks caused by fiscal announcements.

title: Predictive Modeling for Drone Swarm Attack Defense: AI Trajectory Forecasting and Optimal Intercept Strategy Design for U.S. Military Readiness
affiliations: University of the Cumberlands

detail.title: Predictive Modeling for Drone Swarm Attack Defense: AI Trajectory Forecasting and Optimal Intercept Strategy Design for U.S. Military Readiness
detail.abstract: This research investigates the application of advanced machine learning techniquesincluding Reinforcement Learning (RL), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and multi-agent simulation-to predict drone swarm trajectories and optimize defensive intercept strategies. Drone swarms represent one of the most rapidly advancing and strategically significant threats to U.S. airbases, naval fleets, and forward-operating installations. By modeling swarm maneuvers validated against real-world demonstrations from China, the United States, Russia, and Iran, this study demonstrates that predictive AI systems can reliably forecast swarm behavior and significantly improve intercept success rates. The research introduces an integrated architecture that combines multi-sensor fusion, decentralized swarm prediction, reinforcement-learning decision engines, and layered defensive strategies involving electronic warfare, directed-energy weapons, and kinetic interceptors. Results show that RL-based models outperform traditional LSTM and GNN approaches in forecasting emergent swarm behaviors and identifying optimal defensive responses under resource and time constraints. This work provides a technically rigorous and operationally relevant foundation for AIenabled counter-swarm systems, aligning with multiple Department of Defense modernization initiatives, including Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2), autonomous systems integration, and counter-UAS resilience.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Peer-Level Consultant in Surgery: Automation Bias, Human Judgment, and Legal Accountability

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Peer-Level Consultant in Surgery: Automation Bias, Human Judgment, and Legal Accountability

keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Healthcare AI; Automation Bias; Medical Liability; Health Law; Human Judgment; Clinical Decision Support; AI Governance; EU AI Act; FDA Regulation

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed as decision support tools in high-risk clinical environments, yet their influence on expert judgment and their implications for legal accountability remain poorly understood. This paper examines how artificial intelligence alters professional decision-making and how that alteration challenges existing doctrines of medical liability and standard of care. Using a controlled comparative design, a senior subspecialist surgeon and a multimodal large language model were evaluated on high-complexity board-level surgical questions. Although both achieved identical overall accuracy, qualitative divergence analysis revealed distinct cognitive roles. The artificial intelligence system demonstrated superior semantic precision and strict adherence to textual decision rules, while the human expert outperformed in visual interpretation and clinical safety judgment. Critically, the study documents a clear instance of automation bias in which the human expert deferred to a confident but incorrect artificial intelligence output, resulting in an automation-induced deference error. These findings have direct legal significance. They demonstrate how artificial intelligence can function as a persuasive cognitive actor that reshapes professional judgment without bearing legal responsibility for outcomes. The analysis situates this phenomenon within contemporary frameworks of medical malpractice, product liability, and the erosion of the learned intermediary doctrine, as well as emerging regulatory approaches in the United States and the European Union. The paper proposes a Parallel Review model in which artificial intelligence serves as a precision check rather than a decision authority, preserving human accountability while mitigating automation bias.

detail.abstract: We examine the evolution of equity capital in the U.S. banking industry over the past 35 years. Earnings are the major driver of increases in equity capital in the banking industry. While common stock issuance is frequent, amounts issued are generally small and do not contribute meaningfully to equity capital growth in most cases. Common stock dividends and repurchases are significant drains on equity capital. It is not uncommon for banks to pay out more than they earn, driven both by capital planning motivations and negative shocks to earnings. It is also common for banks to both issue new common stock and make repurchases in the same year, with these offsetting actions related to employee stock-based compensation.

detail.abstract: We develop an empirical application on a large dataset of European stock returns, in order to estimate the risk premia. We propose an application of the Three-Pass Estimation Method (3PEM) by Xiu and Giglio (2021) as a multipurpose tool in asset pricing. By assuming the Fama-French Five-Factor model (Fama and French (2015)) as baseline model, we show that the 3PEM yields risk premium estimates that are more economically plausible and statistically robust than those obtained using the traditional two-pass estimation method (2PEM). Moreover, we extend the results by Xiu and Giglio (2021) showing that the 3PEM is able to detect noise in tradable factors. Furthermore, the method is used to denoise the observed factors, providing purified versions that better capture the systematic components of risk. We also identify noisy factors, and yield denoised factor series that improve the estimation of stock-level exposures and expected returns.

detail.abstract: How do interest rates influence firms' export decisions? We first develop a dynamic model of heterogeneous firms that highlights two key mechanisms: (i) a time lag between export costs and revenues, and (ii) the accumulation of organizational capital. Higher interest rates reduce both the extensive and intensive margins of exporting, the more so for firms with lower organizational capital. We then test these predictions using panel data on Portuguese firms (2008-2021). Our results show that organizational capital mitigates the adverse effect of higher interest rates, and this result is robust to alternative estimation strategies designed to address potential identification concerns. We also show that the magnitude of this mitigating effect depends on firm characteristics shaping access to external funding, i.e., leverage, asset tangibility, and profitability.

detail.abstract: The intensification of globalization and the rapid advancement of the digital age require a necessary reassessment of state sovereignty in light of contemporary technological transformations. This study investigates the central question of whether digital sovereignty, due to its transnational and decentralized nature, will replace traditional state sovereignty or, alternatively, transform it, leading to the emergence of a new hybrid model of global governance. Growing digital interdependence, coupled with the dilution of borders in cyberspace, challenges the classic paradigms of jurisdiction and territorial control, causing tensions between national autonomy and new forms of digital power. The objective is to examine the relationship between digital and state sovereignty, outlining their conceptual contours, their convergences and disagreements, as well as their possible forms of coexistence. The analysis focuses on the effects of globalization on the authority of states, especially in the face of the actions of non-state actors, such as large technology corporations, and the growing cyber vulnerability that compromises the security and privacy of national data. The implications of technological dependence and the complexity of international jurisdiction in cyberspace are also considered, in addition to the normative responses and protection strategies adopted by different states. The hypothesis formulated maintains that digital sovereignty does not extinguish state sovereignty, but requires its reconfiguration and constant adaptation. The resulting scenario points to a model of shared governance, in which states remain central actors but need to develop mechanisms for international cooperation, normative coordination, and strengthening their technical capacity to preserve their autonomy amid globalized digital flows. The methodology adopted is qualitative, based on bibliographic research and a critical review of the specialized literature in international law, political science, international relations, and technology. The interpretive analysis seeks to identify fundamental concepts, prevailing theories, and the main academic and institutional debates on digital sovereignty and its relationship with the contemporary power structure. It concludes that digital sovereignty imposes a process of structural adaptation on state power, requiring new forms of regulation and international coordination. Thus, the 21st century governance will depend on the ability of states to balance their traditional authority with the imperatives of a constantly changing digital order.

title: Ecosystem Services Demand in Social-Ecological Systems: Towards a Typology of Assessment Approaches
affiliations: Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM)

detail.title: Ecosystem Services Demand in Social-Ecological Systems: Towards a Typology of Assessment Approaches
detail.abstract: Assessing ecosystem service (ES) demand remains conceptually fragmented and methodologically inconsistent in social-ecological systems (SES) research due to the lack of a framework linking human preferences to benefits derived from ES fruition. This study develops a systematic typology of ES demand assessment based on an integrative review of empirical studies. We conceptualize demand as emerging from two competing modalities: the consumption of provisioning and cultural services, which may drive ecosystem depletion, and the need for risk reduction through regulating services, which supports ecosystem preservation. Building on this distinction, we identify five valuation approaches, two that directly translate ES value into realized benefits and three that infer demand indirectly through monetary estimation, expert knowledge, or threshold-based criteria. The framework clarifies how socioeconomic variables represent human preferences and needs, revealing the diversity and underlying logic of current demand assessment practices. Limitations include the lack of analysis of interactions between demand modalities, the treatment of services in isolation rather than as interdependent bundles, and the neglect of temporal and spatial dimensions. By systematizing fragmented methodologies, the framework advances understanding of ES demand and provides a structured basis for selecting appropriate demand assessment approaches across diverse SES contexts.
