detail.title: Cyber Vulnerabilities at Large US Financial Institutions and Their Third-Party Service Providers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-103, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.103]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper examines cyber vulnerabilities across the 100 largest US banks, non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), and their third-party service providers. Our analysis, based on a proprietary cyber risk analytics model, shows NBFIs exhibit greater cyber vulnerabilities than banks, though banks face larger relative losses from routine incidents. We identify third-party service providers as a hidden cyber fault line in the financial system, often having greater vulnerabilities than the institutions they serve and creating systemic risks. Scenario analyses of catastrophic cyber events targeting these providers reveal potential losses up to about 60 times larger than routine incidents for both large banks and large NBFIs, with business interruptions driving most losses. Our findings highlight the need for a holistic cyber risk management approach addressing both individual vulnerabilities and systemic risks from interconnectedness in the financial system.

title: A KISS for central bank communication in times of high inflation
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, Deutsche Bundesbank and ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research

detail.title: A KISS for central bank communication in times of high inflation
detail.abstract: During the post-pandemic inflation surge, many central banks actively used communication about the inflation outlook as a policy tool to limit spillovers from realized to expected inflation. We present novel survey evidence showing that the ECB’s guidance about the projected inflation path substantially lowers households’ inflation expectations in times of unusually high inflation. A reassuring, positively framed non-quantitative communication style has the largest treatment effects on short-term expected inflation. Providing simple visualizations of the ECB’s projected inflation path also significantly lowered inflation ex-pectations across horizons. We document substantial heterogeneity of these effects along key socio-demographic characteristics. Our findings suggest that, regarding their communication, central banks should ‘keep it sophisticatedly simple (KISS)’.

title: Revisiting gender differences in personality: New evidence on Big Five domains and facets with large-scale samples from 27 nations
affiliations: GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences, Michigan State University and GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences

detail.title: Revisiting gender differences in personality: New evidence on Big Five domains and facets with large-scale samples from 27 nations
detail.abstract: Numerous studies have documented gender differences in self-reported personality, suggesting that women score higher than men, particularly on the Big Five domains of Agreeableness and Neuroticism. Previous studies also indicate that gender differences can vary across facets of the same personality domain. Findings regarding the cross-cultural generalizability of—or systematic cultural variations in—these gender differences are inconclusive. This has been attributed to methodological differences in the samples and the questionnaire adaptations. We therefore systematically investigated gender differences in scores on the Big Five domains in 27 countries based on comprehensive samples representative of the respective adult populations (total N = 143,313) and on questionnaires adapted using consistent translation methodology. Results revealed gender differences in all domains except Extraversion. The most pronounced differences emerged for Neuroticism and Agreeableness, with effects of .40 and .35, respectively. These differences varied in magnitude across countries and were more pronounced in more individualistic countries. Investigating gender differences in scores on 15 more specific, facet-level traits in a subset of countries, we found that typically one facet per domain showed the most substantial gender differences. For example, women scored higher than men on all facets of Neuroticism and Agreeableness, but primarily on Anxiety and Compassion, respectively.

title: Crisis and Recovery: Volatility Spillovers and Systemic Risk Transmission in European Stock Markets before, during, and after COVID-19
affiliations: University of Sheffield and University of Sheffield

detail.title: Crisis and Recovery: Volatility Spillovers and Systemic Risk Transmission in European Stock Markets before, during, and after COVID-19
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped volatility spillovers and systemic risk across European stock markets. Using daily data for fifteen developed European stock markets from 2017 to 2024, we combine the Diebold–Yilmaz volatility connectedness framework with the [[EQUATION]] approach to analyse risk transmission across three regimes: pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic. Volatility spillovers surged above 90% in early 2020, reflecting unprecedented market integration and a collapse in diversification benefits. Large and liquid markets, particularly the UK, Germany, France, and Italy, emerged as dominant transmitters of volatility and systemic risk, while smaller markets acted mainly as receivers. Both spillovers and systemic risk gradually reverted to pre-pandemic levels after 2022, highlighting the temporary nature of the COVID-induced surge and the resilience of European financial markets. The results enhance understanding of how interconnected financial systems absorb and recover from large exogenous shocks and offer insights for investors, regulators, and policymakers concerned with systemic stability.

title: Financial Market Effects of FOMC Communication: Evidence from a New Event-Study Database
affiliations: , , Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and

detail.title: Financial Market Effects of FOMC Communication: Evidence from a New Event-Study Database
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD), a novel, public, and regularly updated dataset of financial market data around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) policy announcements, press conferences, and minutes releases. Using the rich high-frequency data in the USMPD, we document several new empirical findings. Large monetary policy surprises have made a comeback in recent years, and post-meeting press conferences have become the most important source of policy news. Monetary policy surprises have pronounced negative effects on breakeven inflation based on Treasury yields. Risk assets, including dividend derivatives, also respond strongly and negatively to monetary policy surprises, consistent with conventional channels of monetary transmission. Press conferences have stronger effects than FOMC statements on most asset prices. Finally, the term structure evidence shows peak effects on market-based inflation and dividend expectations at horizons of several years.

title: Central Bank Access and Flight to Safety
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Central Bank Access and Flight to Safety

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-100, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.100]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We examine whether access to the Federal Reserve's Overnight Reverse Repo Facility (ON RRP) affects money market fund flows during flight-to-safety episodes. We find that funds with ON RRP access serving sophisticated investors experience about a 1 percentage point increase in net daily flows over total assets during the March 2020 flight-to-safety episode relative to similar funds without access. The effect aligns with theoretical predictions and explains more than half of the inflows in those funds. Our results show that access to central bank deposit facilities amplifies flight-to-safety behavior.

title: Building Capacity in the Public Administration: Evidence from German Reunification
affiliations: and University of Tübingen - Faculty of Economics and Social Sciences

detail.title: Building Capacity in the Public Administration: Evidence from German Reunification
detail.abstract: An effective public administration is essential for state capacity and economic prosperity. We provide the first causal evidence on the short and long-term impact of secondments, a key instrument for building administrative capacity. Our context is the large-scale capacity building in the East German tax administration after reunification, which was designed and implemented in a highly decentralized way. We exploit this unique institutional feature for identification, drawing on a major, novel data collection. Secondments significantly increased short-term output quantity with returns on investment of 1.5–3.1 and had persistent positive effects on long-term output quality. Effect heterogeneity suggests successful transfer of tacit knowledge as the main mechanism behind successful capacity building. Exploiting the richness of our data, we uncover three key design features of effective capacity building: support from offices with strong administrative traditions, intermediate secondment durations, and both task-specific and broad measures.

title: Settlement Speed and Financial Stability
affiliations: and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Settlement Speed and Financial Stability

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-101, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.101]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how settlement speed affects financial stability in payment networks, taking into account netting benefits, liquidity costs, and counterparty risks. Our analysis reveals that faster settlements have ambiguous effects on systemic risk and social welfare. The optimal settlement speed is determined by the network structure and the trade-off between netting efficiency and liquidity costs on one hand, and the probability of counterparty defaults on the other. Notably, we identify conditions, particularly under liquidity stress, where faster settlement can paradoxically increase systemic risk by amplifying crisis severity, even while reducing crisis probability. Our results have important policy implications, arguing against a one-size-fits-all approach to settlement speed design.

title: A Doughnut for islands: Towards sustainable blue economies
affiliations: Universidad de Cádiz, Universidad de Cádiz and Universidad de Cádiz

detail.title: A Doughnut for islands: Towards sustainable blue economies
detail.abstract: The world’s island territories are home to nearly one billion people, extraordinary cultural heritage, and unique biodiversity. Here, we present an integration of the sustainable blue economy concept with the Doughnut of Social and Planetary Boundaries framework. We define a sustainable blue economy as one that meets the needs of its coastal/island residents and its local nature - on land and in the sea - while respecting the wellbeing of all people and the health of the living planet. We assess progress towards this goal by evaluating the world’s island territories (N = 83) using a downscaled Doughnut approach. We track six ecological indicators (relative to per capita boundaries) and eight social indicators (relative to minimum social standards), grouping islands into nine regions spanning four ocean basins and two seas. This reveals a set of 'global North' islands at higher latitudes with high ecological overshoot (average: 300% beyond per capita boundaries), and with relatively low social shortfall (average: 1% below social foundations). We find a 'tropical belt' of islands with lower ecological overshoot (average: 116%) and higher social shortfall (average: 16%). These regional disparities are associated with income-based inequalities, shown by dividing islands into low-, middle-, and high-income clusters. Furthermore, downscaled planetary boundaries can miss important features of local-ecological island diversity; we propose an illustrative 'artificialisation' indicator using satellite imagery as a complementary tool. Overall, the world's islands remain far from socially just and ecologically safe states, with small islands especially vulnerable due to colonial legacies and limited financial options.

title: Counting Jumps: Does the Counting Process Count?
affiliations: Bayes Business School (formerly Cass) - City, University of London, Università del Piemonte Orientale Dipartimento di Studi per l'Economia e l'Impresa and Polytechnic University of Milan - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Counting Jumps: Does the Counting Process Count?
detail.abstract: In this paper, we develop a ‘jump diffusion type’ financial model based on renewal processes for the discontinuous part of the risk driver, and study its ability to price options and accurately reproduce the corresponding implied volatility surfaces. In this model, the log-returns process displays finite mean and variance, and non-vanishing skewness and excess kurtosis over a long period. The proposed construction is parsimonious, and it allows for a simple and intuitive pricing formula for European vanilla options; furthermore, it offers an efficient Monte Carlo sample path generator for the pricing of exotic options. We illustrate the performance of the proposed framework using observed market data, and we study the features of the best fitting model specifications.

title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance and

detail.title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-102, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.102]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We analyze firms' IPO decisions using detailed financial data on US private firms. We find that firms with higher external capital needs are more likely to go public. Following the IPO, firms increase their investment and debt issuance, resulting in leverage ratios close to their pre-IPO levels. Finally, newly public firms borrow from an expanded pool of lenders at improved terms, with a decrease in the within-firm dispersion in banks' private risk assessments. Our evidence is consistent with firms going public to improve their access to capital, which is facilitated by a reduction in asymmetric information.

title: The State of Global Services Trade Policies: Evidence from Recent Data
affiliations: , University of Sussex, , Independent, World Trade Organization (WTO), World Trade Organization (WTO), World Trade Organization (WTO) and Independent

detail.title: The State of Global Services Trade Policies: Evidence from Recent Data
detail.abstract: The economic environment for services trade has changed dramatically over the past 15 years, driven by rapid technological progress that has expanded the possibilities for exchanging services. How has trade policy responded to these changes? How do policy stances in a wide range of service sectors compare across economies? With its unprecedented global coverage, the Services Trade Policy Database and the associated Services Trade Restrictions Index, developed jointly by the World Bank and the World Trade Organization, help address these questions. This paper makes three principal contributions. First, it offers an in-depth discussion of the current state of services trade policies and their differences across 134 economies and 34 services subsectors. Second, the paper reveals how recent (2016–22) changes in policy stances have seen progressive liberalization by lower-income economies but stabilization or even slight policy reversals in high-income economies. This dynamic differs fundamentally from the trend that unfolded after the Great Recession over 2008–16. Third, the paper shows the implications of policy changes over the past six years on services trade costs, and it showcases how the Services Trade Policy Database’s regulatory information can inform trade negotiations, regulatory analysis, and policy making. Alongside these contributions, the paper documents updates to the Services Trade Policy Database’s economy and sector coverage and explains the latest methodological improvements made to the World Bank–World Trade Organization Services Trade Restrictions Index.

title: Four Questions About the Distributional Effects of Climate Policy
affiliations: Leipzig University and Uppsala University

detail.title: Four Questions About the Distributional Effects of Climate Policy
detail.abstract: Addressing the distributional effects of climate policy is one of the key challenges for securing a just and successful transition to carbon neutrality. Leaning on a large body of research, this paper answers four questions pertinent to understanding and counteracting the distributional effects of climate policy: 1) Why are the distributional effects of climate policy important? 2) Why do they arise? 3) What compensatory mechanisms and tools exist? 4) Which compensatory tools should be used? Our focus is on national, intragenerational distributional effects and policy. We demonstrate that, while previous research has primarily examined the distributional effects of carbon pricing, the transition to carbon neutrality, which we refer to as the “climate transition,” generates numerous other distributional effects that are largely understudied. We further highlight that what makes the climate transition different from other technological transitions is that it affects households’ costs, e.g., via carbon pricing, rather than households’ income through, e.g., job loss. This implies that welfare systems in most countries, which are geared towards handling income shocks, are not well-equipped to handle the distributional effects of climate policy. Our mapping reveals, at least tentatively, that those households and individuals who bear the highest relative costs of climate policy (rural, low-income households) are also those who reap less of its material and health benefits and care the least about mitigating global climate damage for intergenerational sustainability. This observation, along with welfare systems that fail to adjust to cost shocks, may rationalize the political backlash. We conceptually posit three desirable characteristics for compensatory measures: they should be efficient, precisely targeted, and visible. We evaluate the policy toolkit based on these characteristics and illustrate how achieving them may be mutually exclusive. While there exist potent and common tools to compensate low-income households, e.g., progressive income taxes, the tools for compensating for the geographical distributional effects are scarce and may imply inefficiencies. In summary, our review identifies several gaps in the current scientific literature and provides a mapping of available policies to help policymakers decide on when and why to use different measures.

title: Beyond image generation. Visual data analysis with diffusion models
affiliations: Warsaw University of Technology and Warsaw University of Technology

detail.title: Beyond image generation. Visual data analysis with diffusion models
detail.abstract: This survey examines recent non-generative applications of diffusion models to visual data, systematically reviewing researchpapers from top-tier Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning conferences, leading journals, and arXiv preprints. Our analysisfocuses on a discriminative utilization of vision diffusion models (DMs) beyond image generation. We provide a novel taxonomythat divides existing applications of DMs into four groups: action understanding, content detection, extra-feature estimation, andrepresentation learning, with further more detailed division within each category.Our systematic analysis reveals that diffusion models achieve superior performance in uncertainty-critical discriminative tasksincluding pose estimation, anomaly detection, semantic correspondence, and depth estimation, but universally face computationaloverhead challenges with 10-100 times slower inference times than their discriminative alternatives.The survey identifies key advantages of diffusion-based data analysis, including a better handling of ambiguous ground truth,inherent uncertainty quantification, and rich representations of foundational characteristics. We also highlight promising hybridapproaches that combine diffusion and discriminative methods that maintain high performance while addressing computationalconstraints. The paper provides machine learning practitioners with systematic guidelines for leveraging diffusion models in visualanalysis tasks and identifies critical research gaps in efficiency optimization and cross-domain generalization.

title: Artificial Intelligence Innovation by Financial Innovators: Evidence from US Patents

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Innovation by Financial Innovators: Evidence from US Patents

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-104, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.104]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) patent rates (i.e., the number of AI patents/number of firms of the same type) and concentration metrics (i.e., the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) and Gini coefficient) among financial market participants from 2000 to 2020. It documents the historical trajectories of AI innovation for regulated banking entities and less-regulated firms, revealing that nonfinancial companies exhibit the highest baseline AI patent rate, while banks show the highest growth in AI patent rate over time. Banks have the highest HHI, and nonfinancial companies have the highest Gini coefficient, suggesting that a small number of banks dominate AI innovation and the distribution of AI innovation at nonfinancial firms � though higher in number � is highly skewed toward a subset of players. These findings indicate that the AI technological gap between small and large banks may be widening and the diversity of nonfinancial companies serving as third-party AI service providers may be limited.

title: Research on the Impact of Green Finance Policies on Corporate Green Technology Innovation: Based on the Synergistic Effects and Mechanisms with Social Capital
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Research on the Impact of Green Finance Policies on Corporate Green Technology Innovation: Based on the Synergistic Effects and Mechanisms with Social Capital
detail.abstract: The positive role of green finance policies in promoting corporate green technological innovation has been extensively documented, but existing research has not fully explored how these policies guide social capital and the subsequent synergistic effects arising from the interaction between green finance and social capital on corporate green technological innovation, as well as the underlying mechanisms. Taking China’s Guiding Opinions on Constructing a Green Financial System (issued in 2016) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study applied a difference-in-differences model to analyze data from Chinese A-share listed companies spanning from 2007 to 2019. The results showed that: (1) In the early stage of policy implementation, green finance policies exerted a certain inhibitory effect on corporate green technological innovation; (2) Green finance policies played a positive guiding role in directing social capital towards green investment areas; (3) When green finance policies and social capital interacted, they produced a significant "1+1>2" synergistic effect in promoting corporate green technological innovation, and this synergistic effect was more pronounced in state-owned enterprises and small- and medium-sized enterprises; (4) Both corporate ESG performance and environmental regulation positively moderated the formation of this synergistic effect through market selection and institutional incentive mechanisms, respectively. This study enriches the research framework of green finance and provides practical implications for optimizing green finance policy design and promoting corporate green transformation.

title: The 2033 Social Security Deadline - Statutory Depletion as a Distinct Mechanism of Fiscal Crisis

detail.title: The 2033 Social Security Deadline - Statutory Depletion as a Distinct Mechanism of Fiscal Crisis
detail.abstract:
The 2033 depletion of the Social Security Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund represents a widely anticipated fiscal event that remains under-theorized in terms of its crisis mechanism. Existing fiscal crisis frameworks, including IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis, Kotlikoff's fiscal gap accounting, Reinhart and Rogoff's historical default taxonomy, and DSGE fiscal limit models, treat sovereign fiscal stress as fundamentally market-mediated, triggered by investor confidence and bond market dynamics. This paper argues that Social Security operates under a categorically distinct legal architecture that produces a different type of crisis.

The Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. § 401) combined with the Antideficiency Act (31 U.S.C. § 1341) creates what I term "statutory depletion": a deterministic crisis mechanism that is immune to standard sovereign debt policy levers. Upon Trust Fund exhaustion, benefits are automatically reduced to match incoming tax revenues by operation of law, not market pressure. The Supreme Court confirmed in Office of Personnel Management v. Richmond (1990) that statutory entitlements cannot compel payment absent explicit appropriation, establishing benefit reduction as a constitutional certainty upon Trust Fund exhaustion. This mechanism is deterministic rather than probabilistic, statute-mediated rather than market-mediated, and produces two simultaneous economic shocks: a debt dynamics shock as Trust Fund redemption forces Treasury to issue trillions in new public debt, and an aggregate demand shock as benefit cuts reduce income for more than 70 million Americans.

The paper further demonstrates that the political economy of entitlement reform, characterized by constituency lock-in, blame avoidance dynamics, and demonstrated legislative incapacity, renders pre-deadline reform structurally improbable. The 2033 date functions as a binding statutory deadline, not a negotiation point. This reframing has significant implications for fiscal policy analysis, asset pricing models, and sovereign risk assessment.

title: Financial Citizenship and Capital Market Participation in Brazil: A Macro-Level Regional Analysis
affiliations: Universidade Federal Fluminense, Universidade Federal Fluminense and Universidade Federal Fluminense

detail.title: Financial Citizenship and Capital Market Participation in Brazil: A Macro-Level Regional Analysis
detail.abstract: This study presents a macro-level analysis of financial citizenship and capital market participation in Brazil using official data from 27 federative units. Unlike traditional individual-level surveys focused on stocks, we examine participation in both the stock market (B3) and public bonds (Tesouro Direto). K-means clustering identifies two regional groups (“Northern” and “Southern”), and OLS regressions with HC3 robust errors show that the Financial Education Index consistently predicts participation across regions. The Municipal Human Development Index strongly predicts participation in the South but not in the North, highlighting structural regional disparities. Results suggest financial citizenship policies should be tailored regionally.

title: A Graded Decision Framework for Rumor Containment: Modeling the Coupled Dynamics of Credit Regulation and Rumor Propagation in Multiplex Networks
affiliations: Xiangtan University, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan University and Xiangtan University

detail.title: A Graded Decision Framework for Rumor Containment: Modeling the Coupled Dynamics of Credit Regulation and Rumor Propagation in Multiplex Networks
detail.abstract: The governance of online rumors faces growing complexity due to the coupled diffusion of credit risks. The absence of unified legislation and institutional support leads to a structural imbalance between two critical credit regulation tools—credit punishment and credit repair, which severely undermines their governance efficacy. To address this issue, we propose a two-layer coupled heterogeneous network model that integrates “credit regulation” with “rumor propagation”. Our model incorporates individual heterogeneity and inter-layer coupling mechanisms, key parameters such as credit punishment rate, credit repair rate and credit risk level are included. Using the Micro-Markov Chain Approach (MMCA) and Monte Carlo simulations (MC), we systematically quantify the synergistic suppression effect of different credit tool combinations on rumor propagation. Our findings reveal that a coordinated configuration of credit punishment and credit repair mechanisms significantly reduces the scale of rumor propagation. In particular, a punishment strategy characterized as “severe crackdown, moderate stabilization, and lenient tolerance” combined with a “graded repair” principle, demonstrates optimal governance performance across diverse credit risk environments. This study provides a quantifiable decision-making basis and strategic support for the refinement of rumor-related legislation and the advancement of scientific governance.

title: How Crowdfunding Reconfigures Young Innovative Venture Financing
affiliations: MBS School of Business and Aix-Marseille University

detail.title: How Crowdfunding Reconfigures Young Innovative Venture Financing
detail.abstract: Crowdfunding has emerged as a digital alternative to “traditional” early-stage financing, competing with established sources of entrepreneurial capital such as business angels and venture capitalists. Entrepreneurs must determine not only which source of external finance to pursue but eventually also in what sequence, and this paper develops a theoretical framework to analyze this choice. We model a two-stage financing setting in which investors compete, and either “traditional” players or “the crowd” may hold a competitive advantage depending on transaction costs, support quality, monitoring efficiency, and venture valuation. The model identifies the entrepreneur’s optimal funding source as a function of these parameters and predicts rational financing round sequences as well as distinguishing characteristics of ventures backed by “traditional” investors versus those financed through “the crowd”. Our results highlight the strategic consequences of this competition: crowdfunding expands entrepreneurs’ outside options, and shifts bargaining power within entrepreneurial ecosystems. Moreover, the theory explains the substitution effect of crowdfunding: business angels and venture capitalists must enhance their expertise, reputation, and specialization to remain competitive in the early-stage entrepreneurial finance market.

title: Employee Approval of CEOs and its Effect on Corporate Innovation
affiliations: University of Warwick - Warwick Business School, University of Bradford and University of Birmingham

detail.title: Employee Approval of CEOs and its Effect on Corporate Innovation
detail.abstract: Corporate innovation hinges not only on technological resources and governance structures, but also on how employees perceive and evaluate top leadership. Yet employees’ collective assessments of CEOs have received little attention as a determinant of firms’ innovative output. Building on stakeholder theory, we conceptualize employee approval of the CEO as a salient organizational signal that shapes the internal conditions under which innovation unfolds. We argue that higher employee approval enhances innovation by strengthening motivation, collaboration, and alignment with strategic initiatives, while its effect depends on governance and environmental context. Specifically, we propose that board independence attenuates, whereas environmental munificence and corporate political lobbying amplify, the relationship between employee approval and innovation. We test these arguments using Glassdoor-based employee evaluations combined with financial, governance, and patent data from 11,198 firm-year observations of S&P 1500 firms between 2008 and 2022. Consistent with our hypotheses, employee approval of the CEO is positively associated with firms’ innovative output, and this relationship varies with governance and environmental conditions. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

title: Decarbonization in Australia’s Mining Sector: An Integrated Assessment based on Scope 1-2-3 Emissions
affiliations: Monash University

detail.title: Decarbonization in Australia’s Mining Sector: An Integrated Assessment based on Scope 1-2-3 Emissions
detail.abstract: Since 1990, rising energy demand and mining emissions have pushed Australia to prioritize decarbonizing its mining sector. However, while the country has pledged to achieve net zero emissions by 2050 and a 43% reduction by 2030, progress in decarbonizing the mining sector remains limited. This paper comparatively examines the decarbonization performance of Western Australia (WA) and Queensland (Qld) which account for 86% of Australia’s mining emissions. Using a literature review and emissions modelling framework based on Scope 1 (direct), Scope 2 (purchased electricity), and Scope 3 (value-chain) categories, the study analyses emissions reduction, technology uptake, and regulatory capacity in both states. Results show that downstream Scope 3 emissions from iron-ore-to-steel processing in WA and coal combustion in Qld account for over 90% of the states’ total mining emissions. Sensitivity testing further highlights significant variability in total emissions depending on allocation factors and combustion assumptions. WA shows stronger cross-agency coordination and progress in hydrogen and critical mineral sectors while Qld has contradictory position between renewable expansion and coal dependence. The findings underscore that without fossil fuel phase-out, renewables have only marginal impact on mining decarbonization. This will require aligning national decarbonization policies with mining export practices. However, the paper concludes that removing fossil fuels overnight in Australia without fully opting for transitional energy sources would require major financial and infrastructural remodelling. To address this, Australia would benefit from a combined approach including strengthening governance coherence, managing its mineral export portfolio, harmonising Scope 3 reporting, and adopting transitional clean technologies.

title: Income inequality and the trade-off between socio-economic and ecological goals
affiliations: University of Siegen - School of Economic Disciplines and Free University of Berlin (FUB) - Department of Business and Economics

detail.title: Income inequality and the trade-off between socio-economic and ecological goals
detail.abstract: No country currently achieves basic social needs without exceeding ecological limits, yet the environmental cost of attaining given living standards differs substantially across countries. This paper examines whether income inequality moderates this trade-off. Unlike much of the literature, which emphasizes within-country dynamics, we focus on cross-country variation. Employing a cross-sectional time-series panel of 124 countries from 1992–2015, we estimate models with Mundlak decompositions that isolate between-country differences. Our results show contrasting patterns: in low- and high-income countries, greater income equality is linked with lower environmental costs at a given standard of living. In contrast, in middle-income countries, greater inequality is associated with lower ecological damage. We interpret these differences through variation in the marginal propensity to consume and to emit, suggesting that distributive structures shape how societies navigate the trade-off between living standards and environmental sustainability.

title: Latent Regimes in Material Footprint Decoupling: EU and MERCOSUR (1994-2024)
affiliations: Universidade do Porto

detail.title: Latent Regimes in Material Footprint Decoupling: EU and MERCOSUR (1994-2024)
detail.abstract: Material footprint (MF) decoupling from GDP in the European Union and MERCOSUR during the period 1994–2024 is examined, addressing a gap in comparative regional sustainability analysis. Tapio's eight-state decoupling taxonomy, combined with a pooled Hidden Markov Model (HMM), is applied to identify latent regimes governing the relationship between economic growth and resource consumption. The material externalization gap (MF–DMC) is incorporated to assess whether apparent decoupling reflects genuine efficiency gains or outsourced extraction. The results reveal fundamental differences between regions. In the European Union, volatile switching between efficiency-oriented and material-intensive regimes is observed (mean duration 1.0–3.6 years), with strong decoupling achieved in 29.1% of observations but frequently reversed. In MERCOSUR, persistent material-intensive regimes dominate (mean duration 9.1 years), with only 19.2% of episodes classified as strong decoupling. The European Union maintains a positive externalization gap (median +0.05 Gt), indicating import-dependent consumption, whereas MERCOSUR exhibits negative values (median –0.12 Gt), confirming its role as a net material supplier. Panel analysis indicates that strong decoupling is associated with gap narrowing (–7.4 Mt/year in the European Union, –18.1 Mt/year in MERCOSUR), while expansive negative decoupling contributes to gap widening (+8.0 Mt/year in the European Union, +14.9 Mt/year in MERCOSUR). These findings challenge narratives of monotonic green growth, demonstrating that decoupling is episodic and contingent rather than structural, with significant implications for EU–MERCOSUR trade agreements and global sustainability governance.

title: Green in Name or Green in Action? Evidence from Chinese Mutual Funds
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, Tsinghua University, Capital University of Economics and Business - International School of Economics and Management and Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Green in Name or Green in Action? Evidence from Chinese Mutual Funds
detail.abstract: Using Chinese fund data from 2018 to 2023, this paper examines whether green-labeled funds are genuinely green and how investors respond to them. We find that passive green funds consistently outperform non-green peers in portfolio ESG scores, reflecting a substantive allocation toward sustainable assets. In contrast, actively managed green funds show no significant ESG advantage. Flow-performance analysis reveals that investors in passive funds allocate capital based on ESG scores, whereas investors in active funds are primarily sensitive to past returns. These findings highlight structural discrepancies in China’s green fund market and offer policy implications for emerging sustainable finance systems.

title: Blume-Capel model: Estimation of a three stable state network for −1, 0 and +1 data
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Department of Psychological  Methods, University of Amsterdam, University of Amsterdam, University of Amsterdam, Northeastern University and University of Amsterdam

detail.title: Blume-Capel model: Estimation of a three stable state network for −1, 0 and +1 data
detail.abstract: An extension of the Ising model is proposed as a viable alternative for data with values -1, 0 and +1. This model is called the Blume-Capel (BC) model, adapted from physics for small networks. The advantage of the BC model is not only the fact that it is possible to have a neutral (centrist) position on the response scale, but also that this model allows for three stable states. We show that the zero-controlling parameter of the BC model allows for different types of solutions, and includes three stable states with hysteresis. We also characterise the BC model as part of the exponential family of distributions and show that the model is identified. We then show that combining pseudo-likelihood with lasso yields accurate parameter recovery for the BC model, even in small networks. Moreover, confidence intervals with good coverage properties can be obtained using the desparsified lasso together with sandwich and shrinkage techniques. We apply the methods to data obtained from the online platform Stemwijzer, intended to aid people in deciding for whom to vote.

title: Commodity Market Speculation: A Global-China Comparison
affiliations: University College Dublin (UCD) - Department of Banking & Finance, University College Dublin (UCD) - Department of Banking & Finance, Universitat Jaume I - Department of Finance and Accounting and Utrecht University - School of Economics

detail.title: Commodity Market Speculation: A Global-China Comparison
detail.abstract: We study speculative trading in Chinese and global commodity futures. Using a heterogeneous agent model, we decompose prices into contributions from fundamental traders, speculators, and manipulators, and estimate time-varying trader weights. Chinese markets have fewer fundamental traders and more speculators than their global counterparts. Among speculative activity, manipulators are more prominent in China. We find a gradual convergence between Chinese and global markets in the trader composition over time. Finally, we relate the increase in manipulators and the decrease in fundamental traders to a decrease in market efficiency.

title: Optimally Biased Expertise
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), University of Mannheim, University of Barcelona and University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics

detail.title: Optimally Biased Expertise
detail.abstract: We show that in delegation problems, a principal benefits from belief misalignment vis-à-vis an agent when the latter can flexibly acquire costly information. The agent optimally succumbs to confirmatory learning, leading him to favor the ex ante optimal action. We show that the principal prefers to mitigate this by hiring an agent who is ex ante more uncertain about which action is optimal. This is optimal even when the principal is herself biased towards some action: the benefit always outweighs the cost of a small misalignment. Optimally misaligned agent considers weakly more actions than an aligned agent. All results continue to hold when delegation is replaced by communication.

title: Comparison of Improved Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Random Forest for Mine Water Inrush Source Identification: Performance in Single-Mine and Multi-Mine Scenarios
affiliations: China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing, China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing, China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing, China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing, China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing and China University of Mining & Technology-Beijing

detail.title: Comparison of Improved Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Random Forest for Mine Water Inrush Source Identification: Performance in Single-Mine and Multi-Mine Scenarios
detail.abstract: Rapid and accurate identification of water inrush sources is essential for the prevention and control of coal mine water hazards. While Fisher discriminant analysis and random forest algorithms are widely applied, their performance comparison and applicability in water source identification under single-mine and multi-mine scenarios remain to be investigated. This study takes the Tunlan Mine in Shanxi Province, China, as an example and comprehensively evaluates the performance of the two models using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix. In addition, a joint discrimination scheme is employed to further explore the generalization ability of the two models. In the single-mine scenario, the improved Fisher algorithm achieves an overall accuracy of 93%, while the random forest model reaches 87%, indicating that the former has greater advantages when data distribution is relatively linear. In the multi-mine joint discrimination scenario, the random forest model yields accuracies of 77–98%, far exceeding those of the Fisher algorithm, demonstrating its clear superiority in handling complex nonlinear data. Furthermore, the results show that model performance primarily depends on data quality and feature distribution rather than solely on sample size. This study provides a scientific basis for selecting water source identification algorithms in different scenarios and holds practical value for improving the level of coal mine water hazard prevention and control. Collectively, these results clarify the conditions under which linear discriminant methods and ensemble learning offer complementary advantages for mine water inrush source identification.

title: Bridging the Gap: Why Digital Skills, Not Just Access, Drive Development in Rural India
affiliations: Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, Central Institute of Post-Harvest Engineering and Technology, Pondicherry University (A Central University) and

detail.title: Bridging the Gap: Why Digital Skills, Not Just Access, Drive Development in Rural India
detail.abstract: Envisioning a developed India by 2047 has driven many policy options lately, including the integration of digital interventions in rural governance. The digital disparities and deeply entrenched structural inequalities can hurt rural India's development targets. In this context, this study examines the impact of the digital divide (in terms of access and ability) on sustainable development outcomes. We used the 79th round of NSO’s socio-economic survey. We constructed a sustainable development composite index (SDCI) using four indicators of SDGs, including safe water, better sanitation, health and clean energy. To address potential endogeneity among SDCI and digital ability, we employed a two-stage least squares (2SLS) regression model and complement our approach with a regression tree model to capture non-linear, intersectional patterns across social groups. Results indicate that both digital access and ability strongly determine sustainable development outcomes. While income is the prime driver of development outcomes, digital ability amplifies the benefits of income, particularly for lower- and middle-income households. Socially disadvantaged groups are performing the worst on sustainable development indicators even when controlling for digital interventions. The study emphasises that mere access to digital intervention and infrastructure is not sufficient. The policy interventions must focus on digital literacy and digital inclusion strategies that address structural hierarchies and posed inequalities.

title: Accounting for ecosystem services impacts - A Social Cost- Benefit Analysis of Wild and Cultivated Seaweed as Soil and Plant amendments
affiliations: Norwegian University of Life Sciences, Norwegian University of Life Sciences, Norwegian University of Life Sciences and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Accounting for ecosystem services impacts - A Social Cost- Benefit Analysis of Wild and Cultivated Seaweed as Soil and Plant amendments
detail.abstract: We assess the socio-economic profitability of cultivating sugar kelp (Saccharina latissima) and wild harvesting rockweed (Ascophyllum nodosum) for producing plant- and soil amendments, including liquid biostimulants, seaweed meal, and biochar. Using a social cost–benefit analysis (CBA), we estimate the net present value (NPV) for six project alternatives. The CBA shows that cultivating S. latissima for all three products yields social benefits exceeding social costs, whereas wild harvesting A. nodosum is not socially profitable. For cultivation, the regulating ecosystem services (ES) reduced eutrophication through nutrient retention constitutes a major socio-economic benefit, while CO2 sequestration has little effect on NPV. For wild harvesting, environmental damage from temporary loss of cultural ES negatively affects NPV. There are discrepancies between what is financially profitable for the firm and what is economically profitable in the social CBA where we account for regulating and cultural ES impacts . Only biostimulants are financially profitable for firms, while all cultivated products are economically profitable for society. For wild harvesting, biostimulants remain economically profitable in the social CBA, but NPV is less than one-tenth of the financial CBA. This discrepancy between financial and economic profitability shows that regulators need to incentivize cultivation and wild harvest firms to internalize the ecosystem service impact externalities of their production. This could be through direct regulation or economic measures, such as subsidizing cultivation for all three products. This way, what is economically profitable will also become financially profitable, and firms will behave to maximize societal welfare, including sustainable management of marine ES.

title: Rates of Return on Private and Public Businesses
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Rates of Return on Private and Public Businesses

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2025-107, 2025[10.17016/FEDS.2025.107]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: Privately owned business assets are an important source of wealth for families across the world, but measurement issues are believed to hamper our understanding of these  firms. We use income and valuations of private firms in the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), first validating the data against external aggregates and then using these data to find rates of return for private firms. With the exception of the years leading up to the Global Financial Crisis, overall rates of return on public firms have generally outpaced rates of return on private firms during the past 30 years.

title: Closing the Gendered Digital Capabilities Gap: Policy Insights from Formal and Informal Employment Contexts
affiliations: and

detail.title: Closing the Gendered Digital Capabilities Gap: Policy Insights from Formal and Informal Employment Contexts
detail.abstract: The gendered digital capabilities divide remains a critical barrier to achieving inclusive and sustainable digital transformation in developing countries. While access to technology has expanded, disparities in digital skills and usage persist, particularly among women engaged in informal employment. Despite this, there is relatively limited understanding of independent digital connectivity (IDC) and how this relates to employment effects in low-middle income countries. Drawing on a conceptual framework that integrates gender, employment type, and capability theory we examine how employment structures—formal and informal—shape women’s digital capabilities and, in turn, influence pathways toward digital sustainability.. Using mixed evidence, we consider digital device ownership and access to internet, and identifying its five main drivers – i) trend and profitability, ii) connecting with prospective buyers, iii) the presence of local online marketplaces, iv) loss prevention and v) low market saturation – we find the need to move from an access-based policy to an ownership-driven agenda where individuals do not fully rely on public goods, other people or resources to have digital connections. Disaggregating IDC into zero, low, medium, and high levels, we discover that informal agricultural self-employment has a higher discouraging effect in medium IDC among men and high IDC among women. In commerce, women are significantly less likely to have medium IDC, while men are significantly less likely to have high IDC. In services, men are significantly less likely to have medium levels of IDC, while women are significantly less likely to have high IDC.

title: Gamification for sustainable mobility: Motivational factors and behavioural changes across two campuses
affiliations: University of Navarra and

detail.title: Gamification for sustainable mobility: Motivational factors and behavioural changes across two campuses
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the influence of gamification on motivations and behaviours related to sustainable mobility across two universities campuses. Based on Cognitive Evaluation Theory, it examined how game mechanics affect users’ intrinsic motivation. The research was conducted through a mobility challenge using The Good Goal, a mobile application that promotes sustainable actions such as walking, using public transport, or carpooling. Over the course of one month, 122 people participated, of whom 91 were active, achieving a reduction of 4,511.5 kg of CO2—351% above the initial target. The results show that intrinsic motivation (fun and environmental commitment) outweighed extrinsic motivation (prizes), and that the needs for competence and autonomy were more satisfied than social connection. Gamification emerges as a particularly effective tool to encourage sustainable habits, especially among young students, although its impact depends on the balance between competitive and collaborative elements and its integration with institutional policies and infrastructure.

title: Navigating Management in the Disruption Era: Digital Technologies as Enablers of Managerial Reconfiguration

detail.title: Navigating Management in the Disruption Era: Digital Technologies as Enablers of Managerial Reconfiguration
detail.abstract: Disruption has become a pervasive construct in management and marketing research, yet its widespread use has progressively diluted its analytical precision and fostered technologically deterministic interpretations. This paper critically examines how contemporary scholarship conceptualises the role of digital technologies in shaping disruption and explores the opportunities, risks, and tensions emerging across organisations, markets, and society. Drawing on a qualitative systematic literature review of peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2025, the study develops an integrative interpretive framework that moves beyond technology-centric classifications. Rather than organising findings by technological domains, the review analyses disruptive dynamics through the lens of classical managerial functions—planning, organising, staffing, leading, and controlling—conceptualised as coordination logics structuring socio-technical action. The findings show that digital disruption is best understood as a cumulative reconfiguration of managerial logics: planning shifts towards algorithmic anticipation; organising becomes platform-mediated and boundary-spanning; staffing evolves through hybrid human–technology roles and competence reallocation; leadership is challenged by opacity and redistributed authority; and controlling intensifies through datafication, real-time monitoring, and anticipatory governance. These reconfigurations produce ambivalent outcomes, simultaneously enhancing responsiveness and scalability while increasing dependence on opaque infrastructures and raising concerns related to accountability, power concentration, and organisational and societal vulnerability. The paper contributes by reframing digital disruption as a managerially mediated socio-technical process and by offering a structured analytical lens for theorising its multi-level implications.

title: Reevaluating Bike-Sharing Efficiency Mechanisms:A Metro Station Case Study in Zhengzhou
affiliations: Zhengzhou University and Henan Province Zhonggong Design and Research Institute Group Co., Ltd.

detail.title: Reevaluating Bike-Sharing Efficiency Mechanisms:A Metro Station Case Study in Zhengzhou
detail.abstract: Bike-sharing serves as a key solution for short-distance urban travel, with rental-return balance commonly used as an indicator of operational efficiency. However, its applicability remains questionable in medium-scale cities with constrained supply. Taking the shared bicycle system around metro stations in Zhengzhou as a case study, this paper constructs a multidimensional analytical framework incorporating balance indicators, metro passenger flow, bicycle usage, and inventory. Using cluster analysis and negative binomial regression models, we reveal the formation mechanism of shared bicycle usage efficiency. The findings indicate that: (1) The balance indicator fails to reflect true system efficiency in peripheral areas, where a low-flow pseudoequilibrium prevails; (2) A significant non-linear positive correlation exists between available bicycles and trip volume, confirming the existence of a critical supply threshold; (3) Urban spatial structure systematically presets the initial endowments of demandpropensitysupply through three mediating elementsmetro station distribution, land-use functions, and the built environmentwhich are then amplified by feedback mechanisms, resulting in a spatial dichotomy of a virtuous cycle in the core and a development trap in the periphery. The study concludes that for cities with constrained bike-sharing supply, operational management must abandon one-size-fits-all balance evaluation and average deployment, and instead adopt differentiated strategies based on urban spatial structure. Urban planning, in turn,needs to proactively embed cycling-friendly spatial elements, thereby providing theoretical and practical guidance for optimizing sustainable shared bicycle systems in similar cities.

title: A Unified Framework for Divergent Markets: The Case of LNG Price Forecasting in China and the United States
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University,  and Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance

detail.title: A Unified Framework for Divergent Markets: The Case of LNG Price Forecasting in China and the United States
detail.abstract: This study develops a hybrid forecasting framework to contrast the liquified natural gas import pricing in China and the United States. We apply the Variational Mode Decomposition to disentangle long-term trends from short-term volatility, adopt a causality-based two-stage feature selection, and employ a component-specific modeling with OLS and Gaussian Process Regression. Compared with alternative models, the proposed approach achieves substantial forecast improvements in both markets. Furthermore, results reveal that China’s oil-indexed and administratively influenced prices respond only gradually to shocks, whereas the U.S. marketized and financialized market is more sensitive to uncertainty shocks, indicating structural divergence in global energy pricing.

title: Synergizing Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain in Financial Risk Management: Economic Implications, Empirical Evidence, and Regulatory Frontiers
affiliations: Cracow University of Economics, Federal College of Agriculture and Nnamdi Azikiwe University

detail.title: Synergizing Artificial Intelligence and Blockchain in Financial Risk Management: Economic Implications, Empirical Evidence, and Regulatory Frontiers

declarations.ethicsApproval: It does not involve ethical approval
declarations.funderStatement: It is not a funded paper

detail.abstract: The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain technology is reconfiguring the architecture of financial risk management, promising unprecedented gains in efficiency, transparency, and predictive accuracy. Yet this integration also introduces novel systemic vulnerabilities and regulatory complexities that demand rigorous empirical and theoretical scrutiny. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the economic implications of AI-Blockchain synergy in financial risk governance, combining institutional economic theory with empirically validated case studies from the European Union and global financial markets. Drawing on data from the European Central Bank (2023), Bank for International Settlements (2024), and documented implementations by institutions such as JPMorgan, HSBC, and Revolut, we demonstrate that integrated AI-Blockchain systems can reduce counterparty risk by up to 40%, lower settlement costs by 60%, and improve fraud detection accuracy by 50%. However, these benefits coexist with emergent risks-including algorithmic herding, model opacity, and crossborder regulatory fragmentation. We situate these findings within the EU's evolving regulatory framework, particularly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) and the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), arguing that the EU is pioneering a "trust-through-regulation" model with global relevance. The paper concludes with a forward-looking policy framework for harmonizing innovation and financial stability in the age of intelligent, decentralized finance.

title: Extent or density: Unraveling the drivers of cropland carbon storage under future socioeconomic pathways in China
affiliations: Wuhan University, Wuhan University and Wuhan University

detail.title: Extent or density: Unraveling the drivers of cropland carbon storage under future socioeconomic pathways in China
detail.abstract: Cropland ecosystems are a key component of the global carbon cycle, with carbon storage determined by both cropland extent and carbon density. How changes in these factors interact to shape future carbon storage under different climate and socioeconomic pathways remains unclear in China. We developed an integrated framework combining the PLUS land use model and the LPJmL dynamic vegetation model to project cropland carbon storage and its components (i.e., soil, vegetation, and litter) in China from 2020 to 2030 under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. Under SSP5‑8.5, cropland expansion drives the highest total storage (17.39 Pg), with soil, vegetation, and litter contributing 71.4%, 20.3%, and 8.2%, respectively, despite moderate density gains (2.55%). SSP1‑2.6 achieves the largest density increase (3.88%) but the lowest total storage (14.72 Pg; soil 71.9%, vegetation 19.9%, litter 8.2%) due to cropland contraction. SSP3‑7.0 shows intermediate storage (14.93 Pg) with modest area and density growth (1.76%). Soil remains the dominant cropland carbon pool, while vegetation and litter respond more to management-driven density improvements. These results indicate that cropland extent exerts a stronger influence on cropland carbon storage than carbon density increases. We recommend spatially tailored strategies that prioritize cropland preservation in the northwest and carbon density enhancement in the northeast and southwest to maximize sequestration while supporting food security and climate targets.

title: ESG Peer Effects under Common Ownership
affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Jacksonville State University and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: ESG Peer Effects under Common Ownership
detail.abstract: This paper examines the peer effects of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) activities under common ownership, focusing on firms from different industries and diverse locations. We find that firms commonly held by institutional investors tend to comove in their ESG activities even after excluding industry and location links. These findings are robust after controlling for endogeneity concerns. We demonstrate that common owners actively shape ESG practices, leading to greater ESG alignment among their portfolio firms through both “voice” and “exit” strategies. Additionally, the ESG peer effects are stronger in highly competitive industries and those with high stakeholder sensitivity. Our overall results underscore the monitoring role of common institutional investors.

title: Worker Preparedness Across the Marshallian Runs Survey Instruments and Early Evidence from the Copenhagen Life Panel
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics, University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, New York University (NYU) - New York University, University of Copenhagen, New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Worker Preparedness Across the Marshallian Runs Survey Instruments and Early Evidence from the Copenhagen Life Panel
detail.abstract:
Worker preparedness is a missing transmission channel in macroeconomics. Alfred Marshall’s taxonomy of short-, medium-, and long-run adjustment was developed to analyse how firms respond to shocks when different inputs can or cannot adjust. We extend this logic to workers by adding an element Marshall’s framework leaves implicit: anticipation. Preparedness refers to the buffers, search strategies, fallback plans, and retraining intentions individuals form before disruption occurs. These forward-looking margins shape both microeconomic outcomes and the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy. The registry-linked Copenhagen Life Panel (CLP) provides a data architecture for making preparedness observable. By embedding belief and strategy elicitation within administrative records, the CLP makes it possible to test whether workers’ expectations and contingency plans are calibrated to the risks they face. Early evidence shows that short-run preparedness—liquidity, earnings-risk beliefs, and separation expectations—is measurable and predictive, and that miscalibration is a key source of vulnerability. The broader agenda is to measure preparedness across Marshallian runs and across the worker life cycle. In the medium run, adjustment depends on search strategies and fallback planning; in the long run, retraining and occupational reorientation determine whether technological disruption becomes renewal or decline. We outline survey instruments for each run that can be integrated with registry data, transforming preparedness from conjecture into measurable and model-ready constructs.

title: The evolution of Zero-Determinant Strategies in Public Goods Game
affiliations: and Northwestern Polytechnic University (NPU)

detail.title: The evolution of Zero-Determinant Strategies in Public Goods Game
detail.abstract: Following the introduction of zero-determinant (ZD) strategies, increasing attention has been paid to their ability to regulate payoffs and influence cooperative outcomes. Nevertheless, how such strategies evolve in public goods game with multi-player interactions has not been systematically examined.In this work, we analyze the interactions between ZD strategy and unconditional cooperator in the two-player game setting, with particular emphasis on the transient payoff advantages and the convergence time toward stationary state under varying extortion factors. Our analysis indicates that, as the extortion factor increases, the system converges more rapidly to a stationary state, while cooperative behavior becomes more fragile and more likely to collapse. However, when multiple strategies coexist in group interactions, extortionate strategies exhibit a strong dependence on population size: they can sustain cooperation in small populations but become increasingly unstable and susceptible to invasion as population size grows. Ultimately, evolutionary dynamics favor strategies that support mutual cooperation rather than unilateral exploitation. These results clarify both the potential and inherent limitations of ZD strategies in complex social dilemmas, emphasizing the importance of population structure and strategic heterogeneity in shaping cooperative behavior.

title: Firm AI assets and its systematic risk
affiliations: Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) - European Center for Advanced Research in Economics and Statistics (ECORE)

detail.title: Firm AI assets and its systematic risk
detail.abstract: We examine how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption interacts with product-market power to shape firms’ systematic risk. A microfounded differentiated-products model with endogenous AI deepening decomposes equity beta into market and technology components and predicts that market power compresses exposure to both, whereas AI can raise or reduce beta depending on use (innovation vs. automation) and the strength of complementary assets. We test these predictions on a cross-section of large, publicly listed AI adopters by matching executive-survey measures (2018–2019) to market outcomes. Two principal components summarize AI: PCA1 (breadth/intensity of use-case rollout) and PCA2 (complements: data maturity, MLOps/tooling, talent). Market power is measured by markups and industry concentration. Across specifications (returns and one-factor betas), markups are a first-order determinant of risk. AI use-case breadth (PCA1) exhibits weak and fragile associations , whereas AI complements (PCA2) are systematically associated with lower beta. Our evidence links product-market structure and AI capability composition to beta  and helps reconcile why technology leaders can be low-beta on market risk while still bearing priced technology/disruption exposures.

title: Exporting, Wage Profiles, and Human Capital: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: Peking University - Shenzhen Graduate School, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and Universidad Torcuato Di Tella

detail.title: Exporting, Wage Profiles, and Human Capital: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract:
Export activity shapes workers’ experience-wage profiles. Using employer-employee and customs data for Brazilian manufacturing, we document that workers' experience wage profiles are steeper at exporters than at non-exporters and, among exporters, steeper at exporters shipping to high-income destinations. We develop and quantify a model featuring worker-firm wage bargaining, export-market entry by multi-worker firms, and human capital accumulation by workers to interpret the data. Human capital growth can explain one-half of the differences in wage profiles between exporters and non-exporters. We show that increased human capital per worker can account for one-half of the overall gains in real income from trade openness.

title: Clayey Oxisol Microstructure and Compaction under Long-Term Cultivation in Southern Brazil
affiliations: Universidade Estadual de Londrina

detail.title: Clayey Oxisol Microstructure and Compaction under Long-Term Cultivation in Southern Brazil
detail.abstract: Tropical clayey Oxisols (Ferralsols) generally maintain stable structures under native vegetation due to continuous organic matter (OM) inputs and strong biological activity, but long-term mechanized agriculture can reduce porosity, increase bulk density, and weaken structural resilience. This study assessed four clayey Oxisols from the Serra Geral Formation in Southern Brazil after more than 60 years of soybean–corn cultivation, examining how chemical attributes (pH, exchangeable Al³⁺, and OM) influence compaction behavior. Composite samples (0–20 cm) were characterized for physicochemical properties and subjected to oedometer tests under stresses from 50 to 1000 kPa. All soils had high clay contents (80–85%) dominated by kaolinite and Fe oxides but differed markedly in chemical conditions. Acidic soils with higher OM and Al³⁺ (Cascavel, Londrina) showed lower bulk densities under load (1.23–1.26 Mg m⁻³ at 1000 kPa), whereas near-neutral soils with reduced OM and Al³⁺ (Palotina, Rolândia) were more compressible (1.55–1.58 Mg m⁻³). These patterns indicate that structural resilience in clay-rich Oxisols is controlled not only by texture but also by the combined effects of OM, Al³⁺, and pH on aggregate cohesion and pore continuity. Excessive neutralization or OM depletion increases susceptibility to densification under traffic. Integrating chemical and physical indicators provides a useful framework for predicting compaction dynamics and guiding sustainable management of highly weathered tropical soils.

title: Cloud Drift Optimization (CDO): A MATLAB Implementation
affiliations: Technical and Vocational University (TVU)

detail.title: Cloud Drift Optimization (CDO): A MATLAB Implementation
detail.abstract: Cloud Drift Optimization (CDO) is a novel nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithm motivated by the drifting behavior of cloud particles under atmospheric forces. The algorithm introduces adaptive weighting and nonlinear drift mechanisms to achieve an effective balance between exploration and exploitation during the optimization process. This paper presents a MATLAB implementation of the Cloud Drift Optimization (CDO) algorithm, which is publicly available on MATLAB Central File Exchange. The implementation has been used as a software reference by several peer-reviewed publications. For the theoretical formulation, mathematical analysis, and extensive experimental evaluation of the CDO algorithm, readers are referred to the original journal publication. This SSRN paper corresponds to the MATLAB implementation of the Cloud Drift Optimization (CDO) algorithm and does not introduce new theoretical contributions beyond the original journal publication.

title: What Would it Cost to End Extreme Poverty?
affiliations: Stanford University, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, San Diego (UCSD), University of California, Berkeley and Stanford University - Department of Statistics

detail.title: What Would it Cost to End Extreme Poverty?
detail.abstract:
We study poverty minimization via direct transfers, framing this as a statistical learning problem while retaining the information constraints faced by real-world programs. Using nationally representative household consumption surveys from 23 countries that together account for 50% of the world’s poor, we estimate that reducing the poverty rate to 1% (from a baseline of 12% at the time of last survey) would cost $170B nominal per year. This is 5.5 times the corresponding reduction in the aggregate poverty gap, but only 19% of the cost of universal basic income. Extrapolated globally, the results correspond to a cost of (approximately) ending extreme poverty of roughly 0.3% of global GDP.

title: Agglomeration, Segregation and Imperial Origins
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Harvard University - Department of Economics, University of Naples Federico II - Department of Economics and Statistics and Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies (IHEID)

detail.title: Agglomeration, Segregation and Imperial Origins
detail.abstract:
What explains the dramatic differences in earnings across locations? We employ an administrative employer-employee linked dataset from Italy that includes the country’s entire workforce to estimate firm-worker or location-worker effects. We also estimate differences in human capital accumulation across firms and cities. We find that the elasticity of the location premia to density is smaller than in other settings and that other locational characteristics, such as segregation in school or the workplace and inter-generational mobility, are more strongly correlated with earnings and earnings growth. Our place-based estimates are similar if we focus on movers who were forced to relocate after the L’Aquila Earthquake. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that density levels jump up at the historic border between House of Savoy-ruled Piedmont and the Hapsburg Empire. Earnings today also jump at the border. This finding suggests that there may be some unintended effects of being a far-flung province of a distant empire, perhaps because of access to larger markets or the administrative and educational reforms that began under Empress Maria Theresa.

title: Who Chooses and Who Benefits? The Design of Public School Choice Systems
affiliations: University of Chicago Booth School of Business, Brown University, University of Texas at Austin and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Who Chooses and Who Benefits? The Design of Public School Choice Systems
detail.abstract:
Public school choice has evolved rapidly in the past two decades, as districts roll out new magnet, dual-language, and themed programs to broaden educational opportunity. We use newly collected national data to document that opt-in (voluntary) systems: (i) are the modal design; (ii) are harder to navigate; and (iii) have participation that is concentrated among more advantaged students. These facts suggest a striking inconsistency: districts have largely adopted centralized assignment algorithms to broaden access, but most rely on optional participation that fragments public education. We study the implications of this design choice in the Los Angeles Unified School District, the largest opt-in system in the country, combining nearly two decades of administrative data, randomized lotteries, and quasi-experimental expansions in access. Participation is highly selective, consistent with national evidence, and lottery estimates suggest that the students with the lowest demand for choice schools are the ones who gain the most from attending. Opt-in participation therefore embeds a selection mechanism that screens out high-return students and leaves many effective programs with unused capacity. To evaluate system-level implications, we estimate a structural model linking applications, enrollment, and achievement. Choice schools are vertically differentiated and generate meaningful gains, but the opt-in participation rule—through high application costs and negative selection on gains—prevents these benefits from reaching the students who need them most. Counterfactual simulations make the design stakes clear: information and travel-cost reductions have limited effects, whereas reforms that change the participation architecture eliminate core inefficiencies and deliver the largest district-wide achievement gains. These results underscore that system design— not school effectiveness alone—shapes who benefits from public school choice and to what extent.
